shiftMode: Call for help early; assign airway, meds, monitor, suction, backup airway, and post-intubation sedation roles.
Preoxygenate aggressively; consider NC apneic oxygenation, flush-rate NRB, NIV, or BVM with PEEP depending physiology.
Have suction in hand or immediately reachable before first attempt.
Choose first-pass plan and backup plan before pushing meds: video/direct laryngoscopy, introducer, supraglottic, cricothyrotomy. Make the first attempt the best attempt.

Name the plan and the action together: Plan A tracheal intubation, Plan B a supraglottic airway, Plan C a final facemask attempt and the wake-up-or-proceed decision, Plan D front-of-neck access. The letter alone means nothing to a room that has not read the guideline.
Maximum 3+1 attempts (DAS 2025): three attempts, plus one final attempt only by a more experienced colleague. Change something material between attempts - a suboptimal attempt is a wasted attempt.
The plus-one is a handover, not an extra turn for the same operator. If nobody more experienced is available, the ceiling is three.
If hypoxaemia occurs at any point, abandon the attempt and prioritise oxygenation with facemask ventilation. Oxygenate between attempts and maintain anaesthesia.
Physiology kills before anatomy: optimize hypotension, hypoxemia, severe acidosis, RV failure, and hyperkalemia when possible.
Confirm with continuous waveform capnography; auscultation alone is not enough.
Do not forget post-intubation analgesia/sedation and ventilator reassessment.
indications: Failure to oxygenate or ventilate
Inability to protect airway
Expected clinical deterioration requiring airway control
Severe agitation or injury requiring controlled oxygenation/ventilation
Cardiac arrest or peri-arrest airway management when appropriate
contraindications: No absolute contraindication in a true airway emergency
Anticipated impossible oral intubation should trigger alternate plan early
Severe physiologic instability may require resuscitation before induction when time allows
Suspected cervical spine injury changes how you intubate, not whether you intubate or whether you paralyse. See positioning.
Adult scope only. Paediatric tube sizing, blade choice, the cuffed-versus-uncuffed decision, per-kilogram drug dosing, and a far shorter safe apnoea time are not covered by this card.
anatomy: Align oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal axes when using direct laryngoscopy; ear-to-sternal-notch positioning helps many adults.
Identify epiglottis, arytenoids, posterior cartilages, and cords. Do not advance through unidentified tissue.
In obesity or pregnancy, ramp aggressively rather than placing the patient flat.
equipment: Monitor: cardiac monitor, pulse ox, BP cycling, waveform capnography ready
Preoxygenation setup: NRB, nasal cannula, BVM with PEEP, NIV as needed
Suction connected and tested
Video laryngoscope and/or direct laryngoscope with working light
ET tubes: planned size plus one size smaller
Stylet and bougie
10 mL syringe for cuff inflation and a cuff manometer
ETCO2 detector / continuous waveform capnography
Tube holder or tape
Backup supraglottic airway
Cricothyrotomy kit available for high-risk airway
Induction and paralytic medications drawn up and labeled
Post-intubation analgesia/sedation ordered or ready
positioning: Place patient ear-to-sternal-notch when possible.
Ramped position for obesity, pregnancy, or poor neck mobility.
Head elevated when tolerated to prolong safe apnea time.
Suspected cervical spine injury: minimise movement rather than immobilise rigidly. Manual in-line stabilisation, jaw thrust rather than head tilt and chin lift, and videolaryngoscopy where available.

Take the front of the collar off for laryngoscopy and have the assistant hold the head. A collar left on worsens the view, and the repeated attempts that follow move the neck more than removing it ever did.
steps: Assess airway difficulty and physiologic risk.
Preoxygenate and optimize hemodynamics before induction when possible.
Verbalize primary and backup airway plan.
Prepare equipment, suction, capnography, tube securement, and post-intubation medications.
Administer induction and paralytic medications when ready.
Perform laryngoscopy with deliberate epiglottis and glottic identification.

Pass the tube under continuous direct or video visualisation. With a hyperangulated videolaryngoscope blade use a stylet, bougie, or flexible bronchoscope. Do not advance a bougie blind at a Cormack-Lehane grade 3-4 view: DAS 2025 advises against it because of trauma and misplacement risk - improve the view first.

Between attempts, change something informed by the last one: position, laryngoscope or blade, introducer, operator, external laryngeal manipulation, suction, removal of cricoid force, or optimised neuromuscular block.
After 3+1 unsuccessful attempts declare 'failed intubation', move to Plan B, summon assistance, and make the eFONA kit immediately accessible.
Inflate the cuff to the minimum that stops the leak and measure it: 20-30 cmH2O. Millilitres are not a pressure - a 10 mL syringe emptied into the cuff overshoots.
Confirm continuous waveform capnography and bilateral chest rise; check for right mainstem.

Secure the tube at a documented depth - about 21 cm at the incisors in women and 23 cm in men, or three times the tube size - then obtain a chest x-ray when appropriate and reassess ventilator and sedation.
ultrasound: Ultrasound can be used as an adjunct for tube confirmation in some settings, but continuous waveform capnography remains the practical standard when available.
confirmation: Two-point check (DAS 2025): the tube seen passing through the vocal cords AND sustained exhaled carbon dioxide on waveform capnography. Sustained capnography excludes oesophageal placement but cannot by itself exclude bronchial or pharyngeal position.
Bilateral chest rise and breath sounds
Absent gastric insufflation sounds
Appropriate oxygenation/ventilation response
Chest x-ray for depth and complications when clinically appropriate
troubleshooting: Desaturation: stop, oxygenate with BVM/PEEP, improve mask seal, use oral/nasal airway, recruit help.

Poor view: optimise position, suction, external laryngeal manipulation (BURP on the thyroid cartilage), change blade or laryngoscope, optimise neuromuscular block. Do not insert a bougie blind at a grade 3-4 view.
Cannot intubate/cannot oxygenate: supraglottic airway or surgical airway pathway immediately.

Sugammadex does not rescue a cannot-intubate cannot-oxygenate patient. 16 mg/kg reverses rocuronium in about three minutes, and the patient was apnoeic before the paralytic went in. Oxygenate and go to the front of the neck; reversal is for the airway you can still wake up.
Post-intubation hypotension: check tube depth, breath stacking/auto-PEEP, tension pneumothorax, sedation effect, occult shock; start fluids/pressors as appropriate.
High peak pressures: consider bronchospasm, tube obstruction, mainstem, pneumothorax, or ventilator mismatch.
complications: Failed airway requiring supraglottic or surgical airway
aftercare: Start analgesia and sedation immediately unless deliberately held for neurological assessment, and if held, say so out loud to the team. Rocuronium outlasts a single induction dose by roughly 35 minutes: a patient who looks settled may be awake, paralysed, and unable to tell you.
Set ventilator based on disease state; reassess plateau pressure, oxygenation, ventilation, and hemodynamics.
Obtain chest x-ray when appropriate to confirm depth and evaluate complications.
Reassess tube depth after transport or major position changes.
documentation: Endotracheal intubation performed for airway protection/respiratory failure/anticipated clinical deterioration.
Consent obtained when feasible; emergent procedure performed when delay would risk patient harm.
Patient preoxygenated and monitored with cardiac monitor, pulse oximetry, blood pressure, and capnography.
Medications administered as documented in MAR.
Endotracheal tube placed under visualization and secured at documented depth.
Devices used: laryngoscope and blade type, tube size, introducer, and any adjunct.
Number of attempts, what was changed between them, and the view obtained.
Difficulty encountered and how it was resolved. A difficult airway is communicated verbally to the ongoing team and recorded on the chart, not left in the procedure note.
Placement confirmed with continuous waveform capnography and clinical assessment.
Patient tolerated procedure; complications, if any, documented separately.
seniorPearls: Your first attempt should be your best attempt. Do not burn an attempt while still setting up.
If the patient is crashing from physiology, a beautiful view of the cords will not save them by itself.
Have the post-intubation plan ready before induction; the tube is not the finish line.
references: Ahmad I, El-Boghdadly K, Iliff H, et al. Difficult Airway Society 2025 guidelines for management of unanticipated difficult tracheal intubation in adults. Br J Anaesth. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bja.2025.10.006

American College of Emergency Physicians. Clinical Policy: Critical Issues in the Management of Adult Patients Requiring Endotracheal Intubation in the Emergency Department. 2025. https://www.acep.org/siteassets/sites/acep/media/clinical-policies/final-cp-pdfs/endotracheal-intubation-cp.pdf

Society of Critical Care Medicine. Clinical Practice Guidelines for Rapid Sequence Intubation in the Critically Ill Adult Patient. 2023. https://www.sccm.org/clinical-resources/guidelines/guidelines/guidelines-rapid-sequence-intubation

Difficult Airway Society, Association of Anaesthetists, British Society of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons, Intensive Care Society, NACCS, Faculty of Prehospital Care, Royal College of Emergency Medicine. Airway management in patients with suspected or confirmed cervical spine injury. 2024. https://das.uk.com/guidelines/cervical-spine-injury/
Verify local airway policy, kit contents, and medication protocols before use.

medicationDosing.indication: Rapid sequence induction and intubation, adult. Doses are targets, not ceilings.
medicationDosing.inductionRequirement: Give an induction agent with the paralytic - never a paralytic alone. Choose the agent by physiology, not habit; see agent of choice below. In shock the two move in opposite directions: halve the induction dose and give the full paralytic dose, because a slow circulation delays onset and an underdosed paralytic leaves you a straining patient at the worst possible moment.

medications.caution: For raised ICP, pain, or tachycardia. Will drop the blood pressure in a patient who is already compensating: omit it or halve it in shock.
No analgesia. Brief myoclonus. Cortisol suppression may carry a negative prognostic implication in sepsis. Halve the dose in shock.

May induce cardiac ischaemia or arrhythmias, and increases salivation. Use in raised intracranial pressure remains controversial. Not haemodynamically neutral in a catecholamine-depleted patient - the direct myocardial depression is unmasked once the sympathetic reserve is gone, so halve the dose in shock.
Hypotension, bradycardia, negative inotropy, and 2-5 minutes to peak. A last resort for induction when nothing else is available, not an equal alternative to the agents above.
Potent vasodilation and significant hypotension. Contraindicated with egg or soybean allergy. Dose on lean body weight, and halve it in shock.

DAS 2025 specifies 1.2 mg/kg for RSI; the lower end of this range gives slower onset and may not give RSI-grade conditions. Dose on ideal body weight. Outlasts a single induction dose by about 35 minutes - sedation afterwards is not optional.
Hyperkalaemia risk. Avoid in malignant hyperthermia, neuromuscular disease, rhabdomyolysis, and stroke or burns more than 72 h old. Dose on total body weight.

medicationDosing.sourceNote: Doses from tl;dr pharmacy, 'The Pharmacist's Do's and Don'ts of Rapid Sequence Intubation' (2023), accepted by the clinical owner and re-affirmed unchanged on 2026-07-30. That source cites no primary references. Intravenous lidocaine and defasciculating vecuronium were removed from pretreatment on 2026-07-30: neither is supported by current evidence. Paediatric atropine is omitted because this record is adult-scoped.
selectionGuidance: Status epilepticus: etomidate, propofol, or midazolam.
Haemodynamic instability or distributive shock: etomidate or ketamine.
Severe bronchospasm: etomidate, ketamine, or propofol.

shiftMode: Confirm indication, site, side, anticoagulation/coagulopathy context, and whether this should be triple lumen, introducer, or dialysis catheter instead.
Use full sterile barrier: cap, mask, sterile gown/gloves, wide chlorhexidine prep, large drape.
Ultrasound before puncture: identify vein, artery, thrombus, depth, compressibility, and safest trajectory.
Needle tip visualization matters. Do not just watch tissue move.
Never dilate on blood return alone. Ultrasound the wire in two planes, or transduce, every time - there is no emergency exception to this step.
Keep control of the wire at all times.
Confirm placement and evaluate for complications per site and institutional practice.
indications: Vasopressor or irritant medication administration
Poor peripheral access with need for reliable central access
Central venous pressure monitoring when clinically useful
Massive transfusion or high-flow resuscitation when appropriate catheter chosen
Temporary access while definitive access is arranged
contraindications: Patient refusal when non-emergent
Infection or burn over intended insertion site
Thrombosis or distorted anatomy at intended site
Uncorrected coagulopathy is a relative risk; balance against urgency and site choice
Do not place a standard triple lumen when the clinical need is dialysis-level flow or rapid large-volume infusion
anatomy: IJ: vein is commonly lateral/anterior to carotid but anatomy varies; verify with ultrasound.
Femoral: NAVEL lateral-to-medial reminder is imperfect; ultrasound beats memory.
Subclavian/axillary access has pneumothorax and noncompressible bleeding considerations.
Always distinguish compressible vein from pulsatile/noncompressible artery before puncture.
equipment: Central line kit with catheter, wire, needle, scalpel, dilator, and caps
Sterile gown, gloves, mask, cap, and large sterile drape
Alcoholic chlorhexidine over 0.5% (alternative agent if contraindicated)
Ultrasound machine
Sterile probe cover and sterile gel
Local anesthetic, syringe, and small needle
Sterile pressure tubing or manometry setup to confirm venous placement before dilation
Flushes for all ports
Suture or securement device
Biopatch or antimicrobial dressing per local policy
Transparent sterile dressing
Sharps container and sterile towels
Chest x-ray or confirmation workflow if IJ/subclavian/axillary
positioning: IJ: Trendelenburg if tolerated, head slightly turned away, avoid excessive rotation.
Femoral: supine, leg slightly abducted and externally rotated if tolerated.
Optimize monitor visibility and ultrasound position before sterile prep.
Place the ultrasound screen in your line of sight, not behind your shoulder.
steps: Confirm indication and choose site based on urgency, anatomy, infection risk, bleeding risk, and clinical need.
Perform ultrasound survey before opening the kit.
Prep and drape using full sterile barrier technique.
Anesthetize skin and deeper tissue along planned tract.
Position head-down for IJ, subclavian, or axillary access so the vein fills and air cannot be entrained.
Cannulate vein under ultrasound guidance, maintaining needle tip awareness.
Pass the guidewire smoothly without force, keeping a hand on it at all times.

Confirm the wire is venous before dilating: ultrasound in two planes - short axis showing the wire inside the vein and not the artery, long axis showing it tracking centrally. If the wire is not clearly seen, transduce or manometer before dilating. Blood colour and non-pulsatile flow do not confirm venous placement.
Make small skin nick while controlling wire.
Dilate over wire without force; stop if resistance or uncertainty.
Advance catheter over wire, remove wire while maintaining catheter control, and state aloud that the wire is out and intact while looking at it.
Occlude every hub the moment the wire is out - cap, clamp, or connected tubing - so the catheter is never open to air.
Aspirate and flush all ports.
Secure catheter and apply sterile dressing.
Confirm position and assess for complications per site and local policy.
ultrasound: Use short-axis for vessel identification; consider long-axis for needle tip tracking if skilled.
Compress vein before sterile prep to evaluate patency and thrombus.
Confirm the guidewire in the vein in two planes before dilation - short axis to exclude the artery, long axis to show it tracking centrally.
For IJ, check lung sliding afterward as a rapid pneumothorax screen when skilled, but follow local confirmation standards.
confirmation: All ports aspirate and flush easily
Guidewire removed intact and confirmed aloud
Catheter secured with sterile dressing
Appropriate imaging/confirmation obtained based on site
Tip at the superior vena cava/right atrial junction on chest x-ray - at or just above the carina; a catheter tracking up the neck or across the midline is malpositioned
A normal chest x-ray does not exclude arterial placement; transduce the catheter if there is any doubt
No immediate evidence of arterial placement, pneumothorax, hematoma, or malposition
troubleshooting: Wire will not pass: stop, do not force; check needle position and angle, aspirate, use ultrasound, or repuncture.
Unsure whether you are in the artery or the vein: transduce it. Waveform and pressure answer in seconds; colour, non-pulsatile flow, and a blood gas do not.

Arterial puncture with the needle only (18 G or smaller, not dilated): withdraw and hold firm pressure 5-10 minutes, longer if anticoagulated. After a neck puncture watch the airway for several hours - a carotid haematoma can obstruct late.

Dilator or catheter in an artery, or any device in the subclavian or axillary: leave it in place. Do not remove it and do not compress. Cap or transduce it so it neither bleeds nor entrains air, secure it against dislodgement, and call vascular surgery and interventional radiology now. Keep the patient flat and still. Removal with external pressure at a non-compressible site risks stroke, haemothorax, and uncontrolled bleeding.
Resistance with dilator: stop; confirm wire path and vessel location before proceeding.
No blood return from one port: check clamp/cap, flush gently, reposition; do not force against resistance.

Sudden hypoxia, hypotension, or cardiovascular collapse around an open hub: suspect air embolism - occlude the hub, left lateral decubitus head-down, 100% oxygen, and aspirate from a central lumen if one is in place.
Unstable after line: consider pneumothorax, bleeding, arrhythmia, air embolism, or unrelated shock progression.
complications: Pneumothorax or hemothorax, especially with IJ/subclavian/axillary approaches
aftercare: Label line and date dressing per local policy.
Review imaging/confirmation before using for high-risk infusions if required by site/policy.
Remove unnecessary lines as soon as clinically appropriate.
Reassess insertion site for bleeding or hematoma after placement.
documentation: Central venous catheter placed for documented clinical indication.
Consent obtained when feasible; emergent need documented if consent not possible.
Site and side confirmed; sterile technique with full barrier precautions used.
Ultrasound guidance used to identify vessel and guide cannulation.
Guidewire passed without resistance and removed intact.
All ports aspirated and flushed; catheter secured with sterile dressing.
Placement confirmation and immediate complication assessment documented.
seniorPearls: Most catastrophic central line errors happen after venous puncture, not before it: wire control, dilation, and confirmation are where discipline matters.
If the wire does not pass smoothly, the answer is almost never more force.
Open the exact catheter you need. A triple lumen is not a Cordis and not a dialysis catheter.
After two failed passes, change something: the site, the operator, or the plan. The best predictor of a bad line is someone past their limit.
If a large-bore device ends up in an artery, the instinctive action is the lethal one. Leave it in and make the call.
references: American Society of Anesthesiologists. Practice Guidelines for Central Venous Access 2020. Anesthesiology. 2020;132(1):8-43. https://journals.lww.com/anesthesiology/fulltext/2020/01000/practice_guidelines_for_central_venous_access.9.aspx
Association of Anaesthetists. Safe Vascular Access 2025. Anaesthesia. 2025. https://associationofanaesthetists-publications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/anae.16727

CDC. Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections: summary of recommendations. 2011 guideline, page updated 2024. https://www.cdc.gov/infection-control/hcp/intravascular-catheter-related-infections/summary-recommendations.html
Guilbert MC et al. Arterial trauma during central venous catheter insertion: case series, review and proposed algorithm. J Vasc Surg. 2008;48(4):918-925. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18703308/
DailyMed/FDA label, Lidocaine Hydrochloride Injection. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=cddb2b22-fce3-8967-6e54-dca3df5ac4b3

shiftMode: Document pre-block neurovascular status before anesthetizing the digit.
Use small-volume local anesthetic and inject slowly.
Avoid injecting directly through infected tissue when possible.
Aspirate before injection.
Give the block time to work before starting repair.
Reassess anesthesia and distal perfusion before procedure.
Work out the maximum in milligrams and in millilitres before you draw up, and say it out loud. The calculator is on this card.
Aspirate before each increment and give the dose in stages. Aspiration and incremental injection are the two things that catch a needle that has found a vessel.
Decide what you will do if the block does not work before you start - not afterwards, when the patient is still in pain and the allowance is spent.
indications: Laceration repair
Nailbed injury
Foreign body removal
Paronychia or minor drainage procedure when appropriate
Fracture or dislocation analgesia adjunct
contraindications: Patient refusal
Allergy to planned anesthetic
Infection over injection path when alternate approach is available
Major vascular compromise requiring urgent surgical evaluation should not be delayed
Patient refusal, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Infection over the injection site
A pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory. Document it before you block; a deficit nobody looked for beforehand becomes the block's deficit afterwards.

Antithrombotic therapy is not an automatic prohibition for a superficial, compressible block. Current guidance asks three questions instead: can the site be compressed, how vascular is it, and what would a haematoma there do. Answer those, and follow local policy - do not transpose a neuraxial interval onto a block that does not need one.
anatomy: Digital nerves run along the medial and lateral aspects of the digit with accompanying vessels.
Injection at the base of the digit can anesthetize both dorsal and volar branches depending technique.
Avoid circumferential high-volume injection that creates unnecessary tissue pressure.
equipment: Local anaesthetic: 1% lidocaine without epinephrine for a short block, or 0.25% bupivacaine when the repair needs hours. Epinephrine in a digit is no longer considered the hazard it was taught as, but follow local policy rather than settling it at the bedside.
3–5 mL syringe
25–30G needle
Alcohol or chlorhexidine prep
Gloves
Gauze
Dressing supplies
Procedure tray for definitive repair or drainage
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation, applied and then left to dry - the drying time is the part that gets skipped and the part that does the work.
Sterile gloves, and for any ultrasound-guided block a single-use sterile probe cover with sterile gel.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you inject. A small block still uses a drug with a systemic ceiling.
positioning: Position hand or foot comfortably on a stable surface.
Expose the entire digit and remove rings before swelling worsens.
Keep the patient from watching if that increases anxiety.
steps: Confirm digit, injury, and pre-procedure neurovascular status.
Clean injection site.
Insert needle at base of digit along dorsal-lateral aspect depending chosen technique.
Aspirate before injection.
Inject slowly while withdrawing or redirecting based on technique.
Repeat on opposite side if needed.
Wait several minutes and test anesthesia before starting procedure.
Proceed with repair, drainage, reduction, or nail procedure once anesthesia is adequate.
confirmation: Patient reports improved pain or numbness in target distribution
Pinch or light touch testing confirms anesthesia before procedure
Distal perfusion remains intact
Spread on the screen is not success. It tells you where the drug went, not whether the patient is blocked.
Test the target's own territory before the procedure starts: light touch or cold in the distribution, and motor function where the nerve has one, compared against the other side.
Give the agent its onset time before judging. Lidocaine is 5-10 minutes; bupivacaine and ropivacaine are 15-30. A block called failed at 5 minutes was never tested.
troubleshooting: Incomplete anesthesia: wait longer, identify missed distribution, supplement carefully with small volume.
Severe pain with injection: slow down, reposition, buffer/warm anesthetic if available.
Poor perfusion after injection: remove constrictive dressing/rings, reassess volume/epinephrine use, escalate if persistent.
Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Work out what allowance is left on the calculator on this card before drawing up anything more.

Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. The options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia. More of the same is how the ceiling gets crossed.
Pain on injection, paraesthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Those three are the warning that the tip is where it should not be, and none of them is a reason to push harder.
complications: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity, rare with typical digital block volumes
Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
Bleeding or haematoma at the injection site
Nerve injury, usually transient and occasionally not
Block failure, which is common enough to plan for rather than to be surprised by
aftercare: Warn patient that numbness will persist after discharge depending anesthetic used.
Protect anesthetized digit from heat, trauma, and biting injury.
Provide wound-specific aftercare and return precautions.
Protect the insensate part. Pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts - they cannot feel the injury that a blocked limb collects.
Motor block means the limb cannot be trusted for weight-bearing, and that is a fall risk in an older patient. Say so at handover as well as to the patient.
Tell the patient when it will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does, not after.

A block does not hide compartment syndrome, but it changes how it announces itself: a rising analgesic requirement, or pain breaking through a block that was working, is the sign. Write that in the notes and say it at handover so the next person is watching for the right thing.
Return precautions: numbness or weakness lasting longer than you told them to expect, new or escalating pain, or redness at the injection site.
documentation: Digital nerve block performed for analgesia/anesthesia of the affected digit.
Verbal consent obtained and site confirmed.
Pre-procedure neurovascular status documented.
Skin prepped and local anesthetic injected using clean/sterile technique after aspiration.
Adequate anesthesia achieved prior to procedure.
Patient tolerated block without immediate complication.
Side and level, named unambiguously. Wrong-side blocks happen to careful people, and the note is where the side gets fixed in writing before the needle moves.
Agent, concentration, volume, and the total in milligrams - plus any local anaesthetic this patient already had this encounter, and the running total.
Needle type and gauge, the approach, and whether ultrasound guidance was used in-plane or out-of-plane.
Aspiration before each increment, and that the dose was given incrementally rather than as one push.
The neurological examination before the block and again after it, with any pre-existing deficit recorded as pre-existing.
The bleeding-risk assessment and what it concluded, including any antithrombotic the patient is taking.
Whether the block worked. If it did not, what was done instead, and how much of the ceiling that used.
seniorPearls: Slow injection is the difference between a tolerable block and a patient who never trusts you again.
Do the neurovascular exam before the block. Afterward, you created numbness on purpose.
Remove rings early. Waiting until the finger looks like a sausage is amateur hour.

Verify local anaesthetic policy, antithrombotic policy, and credentialing expectations for this block where you work.

agents.note: Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than ropivacaine at equivalent doses.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

0.2% gives analgesia with less motor block and is preferred for fascial plane and continuous blocks; 0.5% for a denser block. Epinephrine is not needed - ropivacaine causes less vasodilation than lidocaine or bupivacaine, so it is absorbed more slowly. Lower risk of severe cardiotoxicity than bupivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Toxicity adds up, but the maximums are not interchangeable and two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling and keep the fractions adding to less than one - half the lidocaine maximum plus half the bupivacaine maximum is a full dose, not half of one. Everything counts: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum dose in mg AND mL before drawing up — say it out loud.
Continuous cardiac monitoring and pulse oximetry from before injection through at least 30 minutes after.
Confirm where 20% lipid emulsion is stocked before injecting — do not start without a LAST plan.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

Where it goes changes how fast it arrives. The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, designated by the clinical owner. The drug labels do not publish one universal figure per agent: they require individualisation by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary and is not the same as being safe.

shiftMode: This is an oxygenation rescue, not a perfect cosmetic airway.
Call failed airway out loud and assign someone to continue oxygenation attempts while you prep the neck.
Oxygen from above continues throughout. Leave the facemask or supraglottic device in place and keep delivering; do not stop because you have started cutting.

Ensure full neuromuscular block before you cut. This is counterintuitive in a patient who is already not breathing, but a straining patient or a closed glottis makes the procedure harder and the oxygenation worse.
Landmark before the airway is lost if the airway looks high risk.
Prep wide if time allows; do not let sterile perfection delay oxygenation in a true cannot-oxygenate crisis.

One technique: scalpel, bougie, tube (DAS 2025). A number 10 blade, a bougie, and a 6.0 cuffed tracheal tube. A commercial Seldinger kit is a different procedure with a different failure profile - if that is what is stocked, follow its instructions for use rather than these steps.
Confirm with ETCO2 and chest rise; secure aggressively.
indications: Cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate after failed tracheal intubation, supraglottic rescue, and facemask oxygenation. This is the pathway the card is built for.
Failed airway with rapidly worsening hypoxemia
Upper airway obstruction where oral/nasal approach is not feasible
Massive facial trauma or airway contamination when standard approaches fail
The last three reach the same incision by a different route. The sequence below assumes oxygenation from above has failed and the patient is fully paralysed; confirm both still apply before using it.
contraindications: Adult scope only. This is not the paediatric procedure: below roughly 8-10 years the cricothyroid membrane is small, high, and soft, and guidance moves to a cannula-based technique. Follow the institutional paediatric difficult-airway policy instead.
Laryngeal fracture or distorted neck anatomy may make landmarks unreliable
Coagulopathy is a caution but not a reason to allow death from hypoxemia
anatomy: Cricothyroid membrane lies between thyroid cartilage and cricoid cartilage.
Stabilize the larynx with the non-dominant hand.
In obesity or edema, make a generous vertical skin incision first to find the membrane.
equipment: Number 10 scalpel blade. The curved belly makes the incision in one pass; a pointed 11 or 15 blade invites repeated stabs and posterior wall injury.
Bougie
6.0 cuffed tracheal tube. Larger will not reliably pass the membrane; smaller leaks and resists ventilation.
Tracheal hook or dilator if available
Suction
BVM with oxygen
Capnography
Securing device/tape
Any stocked commercial cricothyrotomy kit is a separate pathway governed by its own instructions for use, not a substitute item in this list.
positioning: Supine when possible
Extend the neck fully unless contraindicated; neutral with manual in-line stabilisation if cervical spine injury is a concern
Stand at head or side based on training and access
Expose neck widely
steps: Identify and stabilise the larynx with the non-dominant hand, and do not let go until the tube is in.

Palpable membrane: transverse stab incision straight through it. Impalpable membrane - assume this in obesity, oedema, or neck haematoma - make an 8-10 cm vertical midline skin incision first, dissect bluntly with a finger down to the larynx, then stab.

Keep the scalpel in the hole and rotate the blade 90 degrees so the sharp edge points towards the feet. It is now the guide for the bougie. The commonest failure in this procedure is removing the scalpel and then being unable to find the tract again in a bleeding neck.
Slide the bougie along the blade, angled towards the feet, into the trachea. Advance 10-15 cm and no further; deeper risks the carina and the posterior tracheal wall.
Remove the scalpel and railroad the 6.0 cuffed tube over the bougie with a gentle twist.
Advance only until the cuff has passed the membrane, then about 1-2 cm more. A 6.0 tube pushed to its usual 21 cm mark sits in the right main bronchus.
Remove the bougie, inflate the cuff, ventilate, and confirm ETCO2 and chest rise.
Secure the tube and reassess oxygenation and ventilation.
ultrasound: Assess membrane palpability before induction whenever a difficult airway is anticipated, and if it is impalpable, locate and mark the membrane with ultrasound before you start.
Do not scan during an established cannot-oxygenate crisis. Once the decision is made this is a palpation-and-incision problem, not an imaging one.
confirmation: Continuous waveform ETCO2

Capnography can be flat in a correctly sited tube when cardiac output is very low or the patient has been hypoxic long enough to arrest. Absent ETCO2 in that setting is a circulation finding: confirm position by chest rise, tube misting, and direct inspection before removing what may be the only airway.
Bilateral chest rise
Improving oxygen saturation if circulation intact
Ability to ventilate without massive leak
Chest x-ray after stabilization
troubleshooting: Cannot find membrane: vertical incision, bluntly dissect with finger, re-landmark.
Lost the tract: do not hunt with the bougie. Re-stabilise the larynx, extend the skin incision vertically, and find the hole again with a finger.
Tube will not pass: rotate, use smaller tube, confirm bougie is intratracheal.
No ETCO2: reassess placement, obstruction, circuit, and circulation.
Bleeding: suction aggressively; oxygenation remains priority.
aftercare: Secure extremely well; accidental dislodgement can be catastrophic.
Once stabilised, exclude bronchial intubation and pneumothorax: chest rise, breath sounds, tube depth, and chest x-ray.
Arrange early surgical or ENT review and a definitive airway plan. A cricothyrotomy is a bridge, not a destination.
Obtain imaging after stabilization.
Document failed airway context and rescue rationale.
documentation: Emergent cricothyrotomy performed for failed airway/cannot intubate-cannot oxygenate scenario.
Procedure performed due to immediate threat to life when delay would risk patient harm.
Neck exposed/prepped as clinical situation allowed.
Cricothyroid membrane identified; surgical airway established using documented technique.
Placement confirmed with waveform capnography and clinical assessment.
Complications and post-procedure plan documented.
seniorPearls: The decision is usually harder than the cut; say it out loud early.
A small timid incision is a common failure mode. Make enough room to work.
Once oxygenation is failing, this is not the moment for committee discussion.

visualAssets.title: Cricothyroid membrane palpation
visualAssets.subtitle: Palpate the thyroid cartilage notch, slide inferiorly to the soft depression before the cricoid ring. This is the cricothyroid membrane — the incision target.
visualAssets.caption: Target: cricothyroid membrane between the thyroid and cricoid cartilage.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Vertical skin incision reduces risk of vessel injury. Horizontal membrane incision.

shiftMode: Confirm side and indication before incision.
This card is the large-bore tube. For a simple pneumothorax or an uncomplicated effusion, a small-bore pigtail is the better device - see the pigtail catheter card.
Size by indication: 28-32 Fr for significant hemothorax, unstable trauma, or a large air leak; 20-24 Fr or larger for a ventilated patient with a significant leak.
Have suction/water seal system set up before the tube goes in.
Use safe triangle when possible; go over the rib, not under.
Finger sweep before tube advancement; do not blindly shove a tube through soft tissue.
Direct tube apically for pneumothorax and posterior/basilar for fluid when feasible.
Massive hemothorax is a call, not a number to wait for: 1,500 mL out, 200 mL/h for 3 hours, or instability with ongoing output.
Secure with strong suture and occlusive dressing; reassess breath sounds and imaging.
indications: Significant hemothorax, including traumatic
Unstable trauma requiring decompression per local protocol
Pneumothorax with a large air leak, or in a mechanically ventilated patient
Pneumothorax or empyema where a small-bore drain has failed or is unsuitable
Simple pneumothorax and uncomplicated effusion are small-bore indications - use the pigtail catheter card
contraindications: Uncorrected coagulopathy is a caution when non-emergent
Adhesions/prior surgery may increase risk
Diaphragm/liver/spleen injury risk with low placement
Small stable pneumothorax may not require tube
Adult scope only. Paediatric site selection, device size, and dosing differ materially and are not covered by this card.
anatomy: Classic safe triangle: lateral border pectoralis major, anterior border latissimus dorsi, line above nipple/5th intercostal space, apex axilla.
Neurovascular bundle runs under rib; enter over the superior aspect of the rib.
Avoid low lateral placement that can enter abdomen.
equipment: Chest tube tray
Large-bore tube sized to indication: 28-32 Fr for significant hemothorax, unstable trauma, or large air leak; 20-24 Fr or larger for a ventilated patient with a significant leak
Sterile prep/drape/gown/gloves
Lidocaine 1% for infiltration
Scalpel
Kelly clamp
Suture
Occlusive dressing
Suction/water seal device
Suction tubing connected
Analgesia/sedation plan
Ultrasound if fluid or anatomy uncertain
Blood products available before draining a large hemothorax in a hypotensive patient
Single-dose antibiotic prophylaxis for adult trauma tube thoracostomy per local protocol, typically a first-generation cephalosporin
positioning: Arm abducted or hand behind head if tolerated
Patient supine or slight lateral depending indication
Expose entire hemithorax and confirm side
steps: Confirm side, indication, consent/emergency rationale.
For adult trauma, give the single prophylactic antibiotic dose at insertion. Do not continue it for the life of the tube.
Mark site and prep/drape widely.
Anesthetize skin, periosteum, and pleura to the weight-based ceiling on the max-dose card; the parietal pleura is where the pain is.
Incise parallel to rib.
Bluntly dissect with Kelly over rib into pleural space.
Perform finger sweep to confirm intrapleural entry and adhesions.
Advance tube with clamp/finger guidance.
Connect to drainage system and suction/water seal as indicated.

Drain to symptoms, not to a number. Stop and clamp - not merely slow - for repetitive cough, chest tightness or pain, or worsening breathlessness; these precede re-expansion pulmonary oedema. General ceiling is 1.5 L in one session.
Suture, dress, obtain imaging, and reassess patient.
ultrasound: Use ultrasound for pleural fluid localization and to avoid solid organs when placing for effusion.
For pneumothorax, ultrasound can support diagnosis with absent lung sliding, but clinical context matters.
confirmation: Air/fluid return when appropriate
Improved respiratory/hemodynamic status
Tidaling/air leak assessment
Chest x-ray or CT confirmation
Document tube depth and output
troubleshooting: No rush of air/fluid: confirm pleural entry, tube holes in chest, and system connection.
Persistent pneumothorax: check for dislodgement, kink, insufficient depth, bronchopleural fistula, or need second tube.

Bleeding: 1,500 mL on initial drainage, more than 200 mL/h for 3 consecutive hours, or instability with ongoing output activates surgery or trauma now. These are triggers to call, not thresholds to wait for - an unstable patient at 800 mL and climbing needs the surgeon already.
Pain: reassess analgesia; chest tubes hurt.
Keep the drainage unit upright and below the insertion site at all times; raising it above the chest siphons fluid back into the pleural space.
Never clamp a bubbling drain except under specialist direction. Clamping an air leak creates a tension pneumothorax.
Disconnection: do not clamp. Reconnect, or hold the end under sterile water as an improvised seal.
Drain pulled out: occlusive dressing taped on three sides so it vents, never sealed on four, and reassess immediately.
aftercare: Post-procedure imaging.
Trend output and air leak.
Analgesia plan.
Prescribe and document suction if it is used. Avoid routine early suction, which is associated with re-expansion pulmonary oedema.
Escalate on the stated massive-hemothorax triggers rather than on impression. Consider autotransfusion where available.
Do not continue antibiotic prophylaxis beyond the insertion dose in trauma.
documentation: Tube thoracostomy performed for documented indication and side.
Consent obtained when feasible; emergent rationale documented if applicable.
Site prepped and draped; local anesthesia used.
Blunt dissection performed over rib with finger confirmation of pleural entry.
Tube placed and connected to drainage system; secured and dressed.
Placement confirmed clinically and with imaging as appropriate; immediate complications documented.
seniorPearls: The most preventable disaster is being too low.
Finger sweep is the safety check; skipping it is how tubes end up in soft tissue.
Have the drainage system ready before pleura is entered.
Do not drain a large hemothorax in a hypotensive patient until blood is at the bedside and a surgeon knows. You may be releasing a tamponade.
Pus does not need a big tube. Small-bore plus flushes is the standard for empyema; blockage is managed by flushing, not by upsizing in advance.

agents.note: Pleural procedures use a more conservative ceiling than infiltration elsewhere: BTS gives 3 mg/kg to a 250 mg maximum, against the 4.5 mg/kg and 300 mg on the FDA label. A wide infiltration of skin, periosteum and pleura in a patient who may already be hypoxic is the reason to take the lower figure.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Toxicity adds up, but the maximums are not interchangeable and two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Everything counts: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.

Know where the lipid emulsion is before you start.
Watch for perioral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste, or agitation while infiltrating.

shiftMode: This card is the small-bore drain: simple pneumothorax, uncomplicated effusion, and pleural infection. Significant hemothorax and unstable trauma belong on the chest tube card.
Size by indication: 8-14 Fr for pneumothorax, 12-14 Fr for effusion, 14 Fr or smaller for initial pleural infection drainage.
Use ultrasound for fluid; confirm anatomy before puncture.
Measure the chest wall on ultrasound and dilate only that far. A dilator driven to the hub is how the lung or heart gets lacerated.
Seldinger discipline matters: never lose wire control and do not force dilation.
Confirm all side holes are intrathoracic before connecting drainage.
Secure well; small catheters dislodge easily.
Haemodynamic instability or suspected major ongoing bleeding excludes a bedside pigtail. Place a large-bore tube and involve surgery.
indications: Simple or selected pneumothorax in a stable patient
Pleural effusion requiring drainage
Pleural infection or empyema - 14 Fr or smaller for initial drainage, managed with flushes rather than a larger tube
Traumatic hemothorax only when the patient is haemodynamically stable
contraindications: Haemodynamic instability, or suspected major ongoing intrathoracic bleeding - place a large-bore tube and involve surgery rather than a bedside pigtail
Significant hemothorax or unstable trauma; use the chest tube card
Unclear anatomy or unsafe window
Coagulopathy is a caution for non-emergent drainage
Loculated fluid may require image guidance or specialty input
Adult scope only. Paediatric site selection, device size, and dosing differ materially and are not covered by this card.
anatomy: Enter over rib to avoid neurovascular bundle.
For fluid, choose ultrasound-confirmed pocket away from diaphragm and solid organs.
For pneumothorax, anterior/superior location may be selected depending patient position and local practice.
equipment: Pigtail kit sized to indication: 8-14 Fr pneumothorax, 12-14 Fr effusion, 14 Fr or smaller for initial pleural infection drainage
Ultrasound with sterile cover/gel if fluid or anatomy uncertain
Sterile prep/drape/gloves
Lidocaine 1% for infiltration
Needle, guidewire, and dilator from the same kit; a guarded dilator where the kit offers one
Drainage tubing/device
Suture/securement device
Occlusive dressing
Flush supplies
positioning: Position based on target: upright/lateral for fluid, supine/semi-upright for pneumothorax
Expose and prep widely
Keep patient still during wire/dilator steps
steps: Confirm target and mark site.
Prep/drape and anesthetize the tract to the pleura, to the weight-based ceiling on the max-dose card.
Measure the chest-wall thickness on ultrasound before puncture; that measurement is the depth limit for the needle and the dilator.
Enter pleural space with needle; confirm air/fluid return.
Advance the guidewire while maintaining control. It must pass without impedance - resistance means stop and reassess, never push - and must extend beyond the catheter tip at all times.
Nick the skin and dilate over the wire only to the measured chest-wall depth. Over-insertion of the needle, wire, or dilator can cause life-threatening injury.
Advance catheter over wire; remove wire while maintaining catheter position.
Confirm pigtail formed and side holes intrathoracic.
Connect to drainage system and secure/dress.

Obtain imaging and reassess.
ultrasound: Ultrasound is strongly preferred for pleural fluid localization.
Identify diaphragm, liver/spleen, lung, and depth to pleural space before puncture.
confirmation: Air/fluid drainage
Improved symptoms/oxygenation if clinically relevant
Chest imaging for position and residual pneumothorax/fluid
No expanding subcutaneous emphysema or bleeding
troubleshooting: Drain to symptoms, not to a number. Stop and clamp - not merely slow - for repetitive cough, chest tightness or pain, or worsening breathlessness; these precede re-expansion pulmonary oedema. General ceiling is 1.5 L in one session.
Wire will not pass: stop; do not force; reassess needle position.
Poor drainage: check kink, stopcock, clot/debris, catheter depth, and whether side holes are outside chest.
Worsening dyspnea: reassess pneumothorax, malposition, bleeding, and re-expansion risk.
Keep the drainage unit upright and below the insertion site at all times; raising it above the chest siphons fluid back into the pleural space.
Never clamp a bubbling drain except under specialist direction. Clamping an air leak creates a tension pneumothorax.
Disconnection: do not clamp. Reconnect, or hold the end under sterile water as an improvised seal.
Drain pulled out: occlusive dressing taped on three sides so it vents, never sealed on four, and reassess immediately.
aftercare: Secure and label drain.
Track output and air leak.
Flush only per local protocol.
Repeat imaging based on indication and clinical course.
Pleural infection: keep the small-bore drain patent with scheduled flushes per local protocol rather than replacing it with a larger tube.
documentation: Pigtail pleural catheter placed for documented indication and side.
Consent/emergent rationale documented.
Site selected with imaging/ultrasound as appropriate.
Seldinger technique used with guidewire control maintained.
Catheter connected to drainage system, secured, and dressed.
Placement and complications assessed clinically and by imaging as appropriate.
seniorPearls: Pigtails are less dramatic than chest tubes but not less capable of causing harm.
If the wire does not behave, believe the wire and reassess.
Small catheter plus bad securement equals accidental removal.

shiftMode: This is a temporizing maneuver for suspected tension physiology.
Do not wait for imaging in a crashing patient with compatible findings.
Use a 14 gauge or larger catheter with at least 8 cm (3.25 in) of usable length. A 5 cm catheter does not reach the pleural space in a large share of adults.
Primary site is the 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line. Alternate is the 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line.
Failure to decompress is common and expected. Have the next step ready before you start.
If you can perform a finger thoracostomy, that is the answer to a failed needle - not another needle.
A tube follows. Assume it, and justify the exception rather than the rule.
Adult scope only. Paediatric site selection, device size, and dosing differ materially and are not covered by this card.
indications: Suspected tension pneumothorax with hemodynamic or respiratory compromise
Traumatic arrest with decompression pathway
Peri-intubation or ventilated patient crashing with unilateral concern
contraindications: No true contraindication in life-threatening suspected tension physiology
Stable patient with uncertain diagnosis should get better diagnostic confirmation when possible
Adult scope only. Paediatric site selection, device size, and dosing differ materially and are not covered by this card.
anatomy: Enter over the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle.

The lateral chest wall is thinner than the anterior in most adults, which is why the 4th-5th anterior axillary site is primary. Mind breast tissue and do not go below the nipple line - that is abdomen.
2nd ICS midclavicular can fail in thick chest walls and risks the internal mammary and great vessels if placed too medially; stay at or lateral to the midclavicular line.
equipment: Decompression catheter, 14 gauge or larger with at least 8 cm (3.25 in) usable length, per the stocked device
Chlorhexidine/alcohol if time allows
Gloves
Tape/securement
Chest tube setup ready
positioning: Expose chest rapidly
Arm up if using lateral site and feasible
Do not delay for perfect positioning if peri-arrest
steps: Identify correct side based on clinical scenario.
Site: 4th or 5th intercostal space at the anterior axillary line; 2nd intercostal space midclavicular as the alternate.
Prep quickly if time allows.
Insert catheter over rib perpendicular to chest wall until pleural entry/air release.
Advance catheter, remove needle, secure.
Reassess immediately, then again within two minutes - a decompressed tension can re-tension on a kinked or occluded catheter - and prepare the definitive thoracostomy.
ultrasound: POCUS can rapidly support diagnosis if it does not delay decompression in a crashing patient.
confirmation: Immediate clinical improvement may occur but is not required for diagnosis to have been reasonable.
Reassess BP, oxygenation, breath sounds, ventilator pressures, and chest rise.

A tube follows. The exception is narrow: the original diagnosis was uncertain, the patient is now stable, and ultrasound or chest x-ray shows no or minimal pneumothorax. A rush of air with clinical improvement means there was a pneumothorax under pressure - that patient gets a tube.
troubleshooting: No improvement: wrong side/site, catheter too short, kinked catheter, hemothorax, tamponade, tube problem, or non-thoracic shock.
Catheter occludes: proceed to definitive thoracostomy.
Persistent instability: reassess whole resuscitation, not just the chest.

Failed decompression, tension still plausible - decide by capability. If finger thoracostomy is available to you, do that: it is not length-limited and works where the needle did not. If it is not available, a second needle at the alternate site is reasonable while definitive decompression is arranged.
complications: Misplacement into soft tissue or abdomen
aftercare: Definitive chest tube, unless the narrow stable-and-imaged exception applies.
Imaging once stabilized.
Document rationale for emergent decompression.
documentation: Needle decompression performed emergently for suspected tension pneumothorax with documented clinical findings.
Site and side documented.
Catheter placed using anatomic landmarks/local protocol.
Patient response reassessed immediately.
Definitive thoracostomy/imaging plan documented.
seniorPearls: A needle is a bridge, not the destination.
If the patient is dying and the story fits, decompression is a clinical decision.
Failure is common enough that you must reassess immediately.
references: Joint Trauma System. Wartime Thoracic Injury clinical practice guideline, ID 74. 2018. https://jts.health.mil/assets/docs/cpgs/Wartime_Thoracic_Injury_26_Dec_2018_ID74.pdf

Western Trauma Association. Evaluation and management of traumatic pneumothorax: a critical decisions algorithm. 2022. https://www.westerntrauma.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/32-Evaluation-and-management-of-traumatic-pneumothorax_-A-Western-Trauma-Association-critical-decisions-algorithm.pdf
World Society of Emergency Surgery / AAST. Thoracic trauma guidelines. World J Emerg Surg. 2025. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13017-025-00651-1

visualAssets.title: Decompression landmarks
visualAssets.subtitle: 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line (anterior) or 4th–5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line (lateral). Lateral approach preferred in muscular or obese patients.
visualAssets.caption: Illustration pending clinical review. Use the visual asset workflow before bundling final artwork.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Standard 5 cm catheter may be insufficient in obese patients. Consider longer catheter or finger thoracostomy.

visualAssets.title: Medial danger zone
visualAssets.subtitle: Internal mammary artery runs 1–2 cm lateral to the sternum. Stay in the midclavicular line to avoid it. The intercostal bundle runs along the inferior rib margin.

shiftMode: This is for tamponade physiology, not just an effusion on ultrasound.
Ultrasound picks the pocket and the path. The subxiphoid landmark route is the fallback for when there is no machine, not the default.
Two situations are surgical rather than needle problems: aortic dissection and post-infarction free-wall rupture. Read contraindications before putting a needle in either.
Have resuscitation, pressors, blood, and surgical backup moving in parallel when indicated.
Advance under visualization if possible; aspirate continuously or frequently.
Small volumes win. 20-50 mL is often enough to reverse tamponade physiology, and stopping there is a decision rather than a failure.
Keep the whole obstructive shock differential active; tamponade can coexist with bleeding, tension pneumothorax, or profound hypovolemia.
indications: Cardiac tamponade with hemodynamic compromise
Peri-arrest/arrest with ultrasound evidence of tamponade in appropriate context
Diagnostic/therapeutic drainage when benefits outweigh risks
contraindications: No absolute contraindication in life-threatening tamponade, with the two exceptions below.

Aortic dissection with haemopericardium: a surgical emergency, not a needle. Draining the pericardium restores the blood pressure and raises the transmural gradient across the tear, and the tamponade was the only thing slowing the bleed - decompression can convert a contained rupture into an uncontained one.
Post-infarction free-wall rupture: same mechanism, same answer. Cardiothoracic surgery now.

The narrow exception for both, per ESC procedural guidance: impending arrest with no immediate surgical option. Then drain in small aliquots, of the order of 10-20 mL at a time, targeting the lowest blood pressure that perfuses rather than a normal one, and stop the moment it does. The aliquot size is a local decision; the principle is that you are buying transport minutes, not treating the effusion.
Purulent effusion or organised clot: a needle and a pigtail will clear neither. Surgical drainage.
Coagulopathy is a caution but may be outweighed by shock.
Adult scope. Paediatric pericardiocentesis differs in needle length, drainage volume, and sedation, and is not covered by this card.
anatomy: Choose between subxiphoid, parasternal, and apical by which gives the largest pocket with the shortest safe path - not by tradition.
Parasternal: the internal mammary artery runs close and parallel to the sternal edge. Find it on colour Doppler before choosing the spot rather than trusting a distance in centimetres.
Parasternal and apical: enter just above the superior border of the rib below the target space. The intercostal vessels and nerve run along the inferior margin of the rib above.

Subxiphoid has the longest path to the heart and passes closest to the liver. It is the blind fallback: 1 cm below the costal margin just left of the xiphoid, about 30-45 degrees to the skin, aimed at the left shoulder.
The target is the fluid pocket. The myocardium is the structure you are steering away from, not a landmark you are aiming past.
equipment: Ultrasound machine with sterile cover and gel, and colour Doppler for the internal mammary and intercostal vessels

Identify the pericardiocentesis kit your department actually stocks and read its IFU before the crash, not during it: component sizes, wire diameter, and catheter French vary between sets, and some sets carry population precautions - incompletely characterised phthalate exposure in pregnancy, nursing, and children is a flagged example.
If assembling from parts: an 18 gauge thin-wall or spinal needle long enough for the chosen window, a 0.035 inch J-tipped guidewire, a dilator, and a 6-8F pigtail catheter
Three-way stopcock, 20-60 mL syringes, and extension tubing
Closed drainage bag or bottle and a securement dressing if leaving a catheter
Local anesthetic if time allows: 1% lidocaine, a few millilitres for a subxiphoid track in an adult
ECG/monitoring
Sterile prep/drape/gloves
Resuscitation medications and airway backup
Sample tubes and culture bottles, so the fluid is not discarded before anyone decides what to send
positioning: Supine, or head up 30-45 degrees if tolerated - elevation moves an effusion anteriorly and inferiorly toward a subxiphoid needle
Expose chest/subxiphoid area widely
Position ultrasound for continuous view
steps: Confirm effusion with tamponade physiology or clinical instability, and confirm this is not dissection or free-wall rupture.
Identify the largest pocket with the shortest safe path. Mark the site and read the depth off the screen before you start.
Prep/drape and anesthetize if time allows.
Advance under real-time visualisation, aspirating as you go, watching the tip rather than the hub.
Emergency phase: aspirate only until perfusion returns. 20-50 mL commonly does it. Then stop, re-scan, and decide whether a catheter is needed - do not keep going because fluid keeps coming.

Before dilating over the wire: see the wire inside the pericardial space. A needle in the right ventricle makes a hole most patients survive; a dilator and a pigtail in the right ventricle makes one they may not. There is no emergency exception to looking.
Place the catheter with Seldinger control, then confirm the catheter itself - not just the wire - in the pericardial space.
Secure the catheter, attach a closed drainage system, and reassess with ultrasound and haemodynamics.

Drainage after stabilisation is staged: keep the initial total under about 500 mL, then drain at intervals rather than continuously. Rapid large-volume removal is what causes pericardial decompression syndrome.
ultrasound: Ultrasound guidance is central: choose the largest accessible pocket with the safest path.
Use in-plane visualization when operator skill and window allow.

Uncertain whether the tip is in the pericardium or in a chamber: inject a few millilitres of agitated saline and watch where the bubbles appear. Bubbles in the pericardial space confirm position; bubbles in the right ventricle mean you are inside the heart and must not dilate.
Re-scan after drainage to assess residual fluid and cardiac filling.
confirmation: Improved blood pressure/perfusion
Improved tachycardia or arrest physiology
Ultrasound decrease in effusion and resolution of tamponade findings

Position confirmed rather than inferred. In haemopericardium the aspirate is blood, so its colour proves nothing - this is exactly the case where the fluid-versus-blood test fails and where you most need a real answer. Use agitated saline, direct visualisation of the catheter in the space, or a transduced waveform: a ventricular pressure trace means the catheter is in the ventricle.
Pericardial blood is usually defibrinated and does not clot in the syringe, and brisk clotting suggests intracardiac blood. Treat that as a supporting sign, never as the confirmation.
troubleshooting: No aspirate: reassess window, needle depth, clot, or wrong diagnosis.

Bright pulsatile blood, or blood that clots briskly: stop, do not dilate, and confirm position. If the needle is intracardiac, withdraw it and watch - a needle hole usually seals - then re-scan for a new or enlarging effusion.
Fluid returns but nothing improves: consider clot rather than free fluid, a second loculated pocket, or that tamponade was not the problem. Clot needs surgery, not a bigger syringe.

Collapse after apparently successful drainage: pericardial decompression syndrome. Stop draining, support with fluid and inotropy, and get echo and cardiology. It can appear hours later, so it is a ward watch item and not only a bedside one.
Recurrent instability: re-scan for reaccumulation, clot, tension pneumothorax, hemorrhage, or obstructive shock alternative.
complications: Right ventricular laceration from dilating or railroading a catheter over a misplaced wire
Internal mammary or intercostal artery injury
Pericardial decompression syndrome: paradoxical haemodynamic collapse, pulmonary oedema, or ventricular dysfunction after drainage, typically following rapid or large-volume removal
aftercare: Continuous monitoring and repeat ultrasound.
Watch for decompression syndrome for hours after a large drainage, not only during it.

Staged drainage after stabilisation, with output recorded. Cardiology or cardiothoracic surgery owns the removal target; output falling below roughly 25-30 mL/day alongside echo showing no significant reaccumulation is the commonly used trigger, and the exact figure is a local plan rather than a rule.
Send fluid for what the aetiology needs before the sample is discarded: cell count, culture including mycobacteria, cytology, and protein/LDH as indicated.
Cardiology/cardiothoracic/trauma involvement depending etiology.
Definitive management of cause.
documentation: Pericardiocentesis performed for suspected/confirmed tamponade with hemodynamic compromise.
Consent/emergent rationale documented.
Ultrasound used to identify effusion and procedural window when feasible; approach and window documented.
Position-confirmation method documented: real-time visualisation, agitated saline, or transduced waveform.
Needle/catheter advanced with aspiration; volume and character of fluid documented, and whether drainage was single-pass or staged.
Residual effusion on post-procedure ultrasound documented.
Hemodynamic response and complications documented.
Consultation and ongoing drainage plan documented.
seniorPearls: The ultrasound diagnosis is not just 'effusion'; it is effusion plus physiology plus patient context.
Pick the safest window, not the most traditional one.
Small amount out with sudden BP improvement is a real win - and it is also the moment to stop.
The colour of the aspirate answers nothing in trauma. Everything is blood.
If you are reaching for a dilator, you have time to look at the wire.
references: European Society of Cardiology. 2025 ESC Guidelines for the Management of Myocarditis and Pericarditis. Eur Heart J. 2025;46(40):3952. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf192

ESC Council for Cardiology Practice. Pericardiocentesis in Cardiac Tamponade: Indications and Practical Aspects. E-Journal of Cardiology Practice. 2017;15. https://www.escardio.org/communities/councils/cardiology-practice/scientific-documents-and-publications/ejournal/volume-15/Pericardiocentesis-in-cardiac-tamponade-indications-and-practical-aspects/

Read the instructions for use of the pericardiocentesis set your department stocks, by manufacturer and revision, for component sizes and population precautions. Cook Medical's pericardiocentesis set IFU is one example: https://ifu.cookmedical.com/data/IFU_PDF/C_T_TTPS_REV11.PDF
Verify local institutional policy, kit contents, consent requirements, and credentialing expectations.

visualAssets.subtitle: Subxiphoid view showing pericardial effusion, myocardium, drainage target, and needle tip entering the fluid pocket.

visualAssets.title: Subxiphoid needle geometry (no-ultrasound fallback)
visualAssets.subtitle: Blind fallback route only, for when no machine is available. Needle enters 1 cm below the costal margin just left of the xiphoid, tracks shallowly under the costal margin at about 30-45 degrees, and aims toward the left shoulder.
visualAssets.caption: Replace assetName with reviewed artwork when available.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: With ultrasound available, the safest pocket sets the trajectory, not this geometry. Steep or deep trajectories risk myocardium or liver.

agents.note: Epinephrine buys a higher ceiling and a drier field. Avoid it in an end-arterial field unless local policy says otherwise.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than lidocaine or ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Toxicity adds up, but the maximums are not interchangeable and two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling and keep the fractions adding to less than one - half the lidocaine maximum plus half the bupivacaine maximum is a full dose, not half of one. Everything counts: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

Where it goes changes how fast it arrives. The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, designated by the clinical owner. The drug labels do not publish one universal figure per agent: they require individualisation by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary and is not the same as being safe.

shiftMode: Use when unstable bradycardia is not responding or needs bridge therapy.
Keep transcutaneous pacing and pressors running while placing if unstable.
Know the generator before you need it: rate, output in mA, sensitivity, battery, and which cable mates it to this catheter. The connector is the commonest thing missing from the trolley.
Electrical capture is not enough; confirm mechanical capture with pulse/BP/arterial waveform.
Spikes with no capture at maximum output is not a generator problem. The catheter is not where you think it is - reposition rather than climbing the output.
Secure catheter and generator carefully; dislodgement is common.
Do not remove backup pads or pressors until capture is reliable and the catheter is secured.
Shortest dwell that reaches definitive care. Review the need daily, and preserve the side the permanent device will want.
indications: Unstable bradycardia refractory to medications/transcutaneous pacing
High-grade AV block with instability
Reversible bradycardia - drug toxicity, hyperkalaemia, Lyme carditis, myocarditis - where pacing bridges to resolution
Bridge to permanent pacing or definitive management
contraindications: No absolute contraindication in life-threatening bradycardia
Prosthetic tricuspid valve - a pacing lead cannot be floated across a mechanical tricuspid
Severe agitation may require sedation/airway planning
Infection or thrombus at access site affects site selection
Adult scope.
anatomy: Right internal jugular is the preferred route: the straightest and shortest course to the right ventricle, and the least likely to displace.
Left subclavian is the second choice for a longer dwell. Avoid an intrathoracic subclavian puncture - it risks pneumothorax and it compromises the vein a permanent device may need.
Femoral works and is sometimes the only option, but it carries higher infection and thrombosis rates and loses capture with leg movement.
Preserve the side planned for the permanent pacemaker. Ask, if there is anyone to ask.
The balloon-tipped catheter floats with blood flow toward the RV when advanced correctly. From the right internal jugular the right ventricle is typically at about 30-35 cm.
ECG changes and capture help guide placement.
equipment: Central venous introducer sized to this pacing catheter - check the French compatibility, not just that both are in the tray
Balloon-tipped pacing catheter with its sterile contamination sleeve and locking mechanism
Pacing generator with battery checked, and the specific connector cable that mates it to this catheter

Named locally: which catheter, which generator, which cable, and the balloon inflation volume from that catheter's instructions for use. Balloon capacity and connector type vary between manufacturers and this is not a bedside guess.
A syringe of air for the balloon - air only, never fluid or contrast
Sterile setup
Monitor/defib pads
Ultrasound for venous access
Flushes
Suture/securement
Pressors and transcutaneous pacing available
positioning: Supine
Sterile central line position based on chosen access site
Defib pads on patient
steps: Obtain central venous access and place the introducer.
Test the balloon before it goes in, then connect the pacing catheter to the generator and confirm it paces.
Set the generator before insertion: rate about 60-80 or above the patient's own rate, output high to start at around 5-10 mA, and the mode the rhythm calls for.
Inflate the balloon with the volume this catheter's instructions state - typically of the order of 1.0-1.5 mL of air - once the tip is past the introducer and never inside it.

Advance gently while watching the ECG for ectopy and capture. Never advance against resistance, and never advance or withdraw with the balloon inflated against resistance. The catheter is not a guidewire and it will find a valve.

Capture, then find the threshold: reduce the output until capture is lost, note that number, and set the output at two to three times it. A threshold above roughly 2 mA in a well-positioned catheter is a positioning problem, not a setting.
Confirm mechanical capture with pulse, blood pressure, or arterial waveform. Electrical capture alone is the fake success this procedure is known for.
Deflate the balloon, secure the catheter and the generator, and obtain a chest radiograph for position, depth, and pneumothorax.
Record rate, output, threshold, sensitivity, and insertion depth, so the next person can tell whether anything has moved.
ultrasound: Ultrasound helps obtain venous access and may help assess catheter course/complications.
Fluoroscopy is ideal when available but often not available in ED crash context.
confirmation: Electrical capture on ECG
Mechanical capture with palpable pulse/BP/arterial waveform
Improved perfusion/mental status
Chest x-ray for catheter position, depth, and complications
Diaphragmatic pacing or hiccups means the tip is against the diaphragmatic surface or through the wall. Reassess position rather than accepting it.
troubleshooting: No capture at maximum output: this is position, not power. Deflate, withdraw a few centimetres, reinflate, and refloat - and keep transcutaneous pacing and pressors going while you do.
Intermittent capture: secure, reposition, increase output margin.
Threshold rising over hours: the catheter is migrating or the tip is becoming inflamed. Recheck position and securement, and hand that number over to the next team.
Ventricular ectopy: withdraw/reposition if irritating myocardium.
Sudden hypotension after a good capture: think right ventricular perforation and tamponade. Scan.
Hypotension despite capture: reassess rate, shock, medications, and mechanical complications.
complications: Bleeding or haematoma at the access site
Catheter-related bloodstream infection, which scales with dwell time
aftercare: Continuous monitoring.
Cardiology/ICU admission and permanent pacer planning if indicated.
Review the need every day and document the plan. Dwell time drives infection, thrombosis, and displacement, and the answer is almost always to reach a permanent device or fix the reversible cause.
Repeat capture checks after movement/transport.
Keep transcutaneous pacing capability and pressors immediately available for the whole dwell, not just for the insertion.
Secure generator and catheter to prevent accidental migration.
documentation: Transvenous pacemaker placed for unstable bradycardia/conduction disease.
Consent/emergent rationale documented.
Venous access obtained using documented site/technique, and the reason that site was chosen.
Catheter, generator, and connector cable identified by name.
Pacing catheter advanced and capture achieved at documented rate, output, threshold, sensitivity, and insertion depth.
Mechanical capture confirmed clinically/hemodynamically.
Catheter secured; imaging, dwell-time plan, and consultation documented.
seniorPearls: The most common fake success is seeing spikes and forgetting to check a pulse.
Air in the balloon. Not saline, not contrast.
Write the threshold down. A number nobody recorded cannot be compared with tomorrow's.
Keep pads on until the whole setup is stable and secured.
Every movement can lose capture; check after transport.
references: American Heart Association. Part 9: Adult Advanced Life Support, 2025 CPR and ECC Guidelines. 2025. https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support
Glikson M, et al. 2021 ESC Guidelines on cardiac pacing and cardiac resynchronization therapy. Eur Heart J. 2021;42(35):3427-3520. https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehab364

Read the instructions for use of the pacing catheter and external generator your department stocks for balloon inflation volume, introducer compatibility, and connector type, and record which cable joins them. Teleflex Arrow temporary pacing catheters are one example: https://www.teleflex.us.com/usa/en/product-areas/interventional/cardiac-diagnostics/pacing-catheters-and-kits/index.html
Verify local institutional policy, kit contents, consent requirements, and credentialing expectations.
