shiftMode: This is an airway procedure wearing a comfort-procedure costume.

Adult moderate-to-deep sedation in the ED or ICU. Not general anaesthesia, not elective or outpatient sedation, and not paediatric sedation - each carries different staffing, monitoring, fasting, and recovery rules.
Sedation is a continuum and you get the depth you get, not the depth you intended. Be staffed and equipped to rescue a patient one level deeper than you are aiming for.
A dedicated clinician monitors the patient and does nothing else. The proceduralist cannot do it: during a reduction your hands are committed and your eyes are on the joint.
Pre-brief airway risk, hemodynamics, meds, dose plan, and rescue plan.

Continuous pulse oximetry, cardiac monitoring, blood pressure cycling, and continuous waveform capnography. Capnography is required, not optional: on supplemental oxygen the saturation is a lagging indicator by minutes, which is the whole reason you preoxygenated.
Have suction, BVM, airway adjuncts, and reversal/rescue meds physically in the room.
Do not give more medication because the room is impatient; dose to patient response.
indications: Painful or anxiety-provoking procedure requiring controlled sedation
Reduction, cardioversion, abscess drainage, chest tube, complex wound care
Facilitation of urgent imaging/procedure when benefits outweigh risk
contraindications: High aspiration risk, difficult airway, severe physiologic instability, or inadequate staffing/equipment are major cautions
Agent-specific contraindications depend on medication and patient physiology

Urgent sedation is not delayed for fasting time. The evidence that fasting reduces aspiration in procedural sedation is essentially absent, and delaying a reduction or a cardioversion for a clock carries its own harms.

Elective sedation is a different decision, and so is a patient with a real reason for a full stomach: bowel obstruction, active vomiting, upper gastrointestinal bleeding, late pregnancy, obtundation, gastroparesis, or a GLP-1 receptor agonist. Those change the depth, the agent, the airway plan, or whether you sedate at all - not the number of hours you wait.
Adult scope only. Paediatric sedation uses different agents and routes, different monitoring intervals, and different discharge rules, and is not covered by this card.
anatomy: Airway patency, respiratory drive, and hemodynamic reserve are the real anatomy here.
Know whether the patient will be supine, lateral, or immobilized during the procedure.
equipment: Cardiac monitor, pulse oximeter, BP cycling
Continuous waveform capnography
Oxygen source and nasal cannula/NRB
BVM with mask and PEEP valve if available
Suction connected
Oral/nasal airways
Advanced airway equipment immediately available
Sedative/analgesic medications labeled
Naloxone and flumazenil available. See the procedural sedation apnoea rescue card for doses, and for why reversal never replaces ventilation.
IV access
Procedure equipment ready before sedation
positioning: Position for airway access and procedure success
Preoxygenate when risk is meaningful
Remove loose dentures/foreign bodies if appropriate
steps: Assess the indication, comorbidities, allergies, and ASA-style risk, and assess the airway specifically: mouth opening, thyromental distance, neck movement, obesity, beard, obstructive sleep apnoea, and any previous difficult airway. Airway risk is an examination, not a box to tick.
Obtain consent and perform time-out.
Assign sedation monitor and proceduralist roles.
Prepare airway/rescue equipment before medications.

If the procedure also involves infiltration or a block, calculate the maximum local anaesthetic dose before you start. Sedation does not change the ceiling, and a sedated patient cannot report the early symptoms of toxicity.
Administer medication incrementally and wait for peak effect before redosing. Stacking doses because nothing has happened yet is the commonest way to overshoot.
Continuously monitor ventilation, oxygenation, perfusion, and procedural conditions.
Treat airway obstruction/apnea immediately.
Observe until patient returns to appropriate baseline and discharge/admission criteria met.
confirmation: Adequate procedure conditions
Ventilation maintained by ETCO2/chest rise
Oxygenation maintained
Hemodynamics acceptable
Return to baseline mental status/airway function before discharge
troubleshooting: Apnea: stop dosing, jaw thrust, suction, airway adjunct, BVM/PEEP, prepare intubation.

Laryngospasm: stridor, or silent obstruction with paradoxical chest movement. Remove the stimulus, 100% oxygen by tight-fitting mask with jaw thrust and CPAP-level pressure, then subparalysing succinylcholine if it does not break. See the laryngospasm rescue card for doses.

Vomiting: head down and turned to the side, suction under direct vision, stop the procedure. Do not blindly instrument the airway - the reflexes that would normally protect this patient are the ones you have just suppressed.
Hypotension: stop sedative, fluids/pressors, reassess bleeding/sepsis/agent effect.
Emergence/agitation: reduce stimulation, protect patient, consider agent-specific management.
Inadequate sedation: pause procedure, reassess analgesia vs sedation, redose deliberately.
aftercare: Recover in a monitored area with the monitoring that was used during sedation, and reassess at defined intervals rather than by impression.
Discharge criteria, all of them: back to baseline mental status, protecting their own airway, vital signs at baseline, pain controlled, and moving at their usual level. Not 'awake enough'.

A patient given naloxone or flumazenil needs a longer watch, not a shorter one. Both wear off before the drug they reversed, leaving roughly a two-hour window in which resedation can occur - and the patient looks well for most of it.
Document pre/post assessment, meds/doses/times, monitoring, complications, and recovery status.
Written discharge precautions and a responsible adult if outpatient: no driving, machinery, alcohol, or important decisions for 24 hours.
documentation: Procedural sedation performed to facilitate documented procedure.
Consent obtained; risks/benefits discussed when feasible.
Patient monitored with cardiac monitor, pulse oximetry, blood pressure, and continuous waveform capnography.
Sedation medications/doses/times documented in MAR/procedure record.
Patient tolerated sedation; airway/hemodynamic events and interventions documented.
Recovered to appropriate baseline prior to disposition.
seniorPearls: Sedation fails when the procedure starts before the room is ready.
ETCO2 buys time; pulse ox tells you late.
The safest sedative is the one you know how to rescue from.
references: American Society of Anesthesiologists and partner societies. Practice Guidelines for Moderate Procedural Sedation and Analgesia. Anesthesiology. 2018. https://doi.org/10.1097/ALN.0000000000002043

American College of Emergency Physicians. Clinical Policy: Procedural Sedation and Analgesia in the Emergency Department. 2014. https://www.acep.org/siteassets/uploads/uploaded-files/acep/clinical-and-practice-management/clinical-policies/clinical-policy-procedural-sedation-and-analgesia-in-the-emergency-department.pdf
American Society of Anesthesiologists. 2023 Practice Guidelines for Preoperative Fasting: Modular Update. Anesthesiology. 2023. https://doi.org/10.1097/ALN.0000000000004381
Verify local institutional policy, kit contents, consent requirements, and credentialing expectations.

medicationDosing.indication: Adult procedural sedation. Doses are targets titrated to effect, not ceilings, and are lower than the induction doses on the intubation card.
medicationDosing.inductionRequirement: Be able to rescue a patient one level deeper than you intend. Propofol and dissociative-dose ketamine can both produce general anaesthesia, so the room must be staffed and equipped to manage an apnoeic, unprotected airway before the first millilitre goes in.

medications.caution: Give over 1-2 minutes; a rapid push causes apnoea. Dissociation is all or nothing, so an underdose does not give light sedation - it gives an agitated, undissociated patient. Increases secretions and is the agent most associated with laryngospasm: have suction in hand. No reversal agent exists. Intramuscular 4-5 mg/kg is an option without IV access, with slower onset and longer recovery.

medications.durationNote: lasts 5-10 min; redose 0.25-0.5 mg/kg every 1-3 min
medications.caution: Apnoea and hypotension are expected effects at these doses, not complications. No analgesia - pair it with an analgesic for a painful procedure. Dose on lean body weight and reduce it in the elderly or hypovolaemic.

This is roughly half the intubation induction dose in this app - check which card you are reading. Myoclonus is common and can be mistaken for a seizure or for inadequate sedation; treating it with more etomidate is the wrong move.
Slow to peak. Wait the full 2-5 minutes before redosing or you will stack doses. Synergistic with opioids for apnoea: reduce both when they are combined.
Analgesia, not sedation. Combined with any sedative the risk of apnoea is more than additive, so reduce both. Chest wall rigidity is rare but occurs with rapid high-dose administration.

selectionGuidance: Brief and painful, haemodynamics uncertain: ketamine.
Brief and not painful, patient stable: propofol.
Painful, and you want analgesia separate from sedation: an opioid plus a reduced dose of a sedative.
Haemodynamically fragile and sedation is unavoidable: etomidate at the sedation dose above.
Anxiolysis only, with no procedural pain: midazolam alone.
medicationDosing.sourceNote: Conventional adult emergency-department sedation doses, accepted by the clinical owner on 2026-07-30. The ASA and ACEP guidelines in this record's references govern staffing, monitoring, depth, and fasting rather than specific doses; the figures here are widely used starting points for titration in a monitored patient, not a protocol, and are not independently verified against a primary pharmacology source. Paediatric sedation is out of scope for this card.

shiftMode: Suspected bacterial meningitis: antibiotics first. Nothing about the LP - not imaging, not positioning, not consent, not finding the tubes - is allowed to move the first dose later.

An LP after antibiotics still answers the question. Cell count, glucose, protein, and PCR survive the first dose. The culture is what may be lost, which is why the blood cultures go before the antibiotics rather than the LP going before them.
Check the blood glucose immediately before the LP when meningitis is suspected. The CSF-to-blood glucose ratio needs a paired value, not this morning's.
Position is the procedure: poor flexion and rotation kill success.
Use L3-L4 or L4-L5; avoid going too high.
An atraumatic pencil-point needle is the default. It roughly halves post-dural-puncture headache and it needs an introducer.
Have tubes labeled and the manometer assembled before puncture if opening pressure is needed.
If traumatic or no flow, pause and reposition rather than digging.
Document the neurological examination before local anaesthetic when feasible.
indications: Concern for meningitis or encephalitis - and the LP does not gate the antibiotics
Subarachnoid haemorrhage evaluation after a negative CT taken outside the window in which CT alone is sufficient
Measurement of opening pressure
Diagnostic CSF studies for inflammatory, malignant, or infectious etiologies
Therapeutic CSF removal where that is the agreed plan, as in idiopathic intracranial hypertension
contraindications: Image the head first, and treat first, if any of these are present: focal neurological deficit, new-onset seizure, a reduced or fluctuating conscious level, papilloedema, abnormal pupils, abnormal posturing, or significant immunocompromise. These are the features that make a mass lesion or impending herniation likely, and they are the reason to image - not a routine CT for everyone.
Deferring the LP for imaging never defers the antibiotics.
Stabilise first and LP later in shock, respiratory compromise, or uncontrolled seizures. The positioning alone can be lethal in a patient who is already marginal.

Coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, or therapeutic anticoagulation: this is a neuraxial procedure and the bleed is concealed. It needs a named local antithrombotic policy, because the hold interval depends on the agent, the dose, renal function, and how urgent the LP is. A single interval transposed from neuraxial anaesthesia is not that policy. A coagulopathy that defers the LP still does not defer antibiotics.
Overlying infection at puncture site
Unstable patient who cannot tolerate positioning
Adult scope. Paediatric and neonatal LP differ in interspace, needle length, sedation, CSF volume, and opening-pressure interpretation, and this card does not cover them.
anatomy: Use line between iliac crests approximating L4 spinous process.
Tuffier's line is an approximation and sits higher than expected in obesity and in pregnancy. If the level matters, count up from the sacrum or mark the interspace with ultrasound.
Needle enters midline between spinous processes toward umbilicus.
Conus usually ends above adult L3; use lower lumbar spaces.
equipment: LP tray
Sterile gloves, surgical mask, prep, and drape - the mask protects the puncture site from your respiratory flora, not you from the patient
Atraumatic pencil-point spinal needle, 22-25 gauge, with its introducer. This is the default for adults: it roughly halves post-dural-puncture headache without reducing success.
Cutting (Quincke) needle as the fallback when no atraumatic needle is stocked
A longer needle available for large body habitus
Manometer and three-way tap if opening pressure is needed
Collection tubes labeled 1-4
1% lidocaine and a small needle for skin and deeper infiltration
Bandage
Assistant for positioning - the highest-yield item on this list
positioning: Lateral decubitus for opening pressure; hips and neck flexed but the airway comfortable
Sitting-flexed improves success and midline identification but makes opening pressure uninterpretable. If you need a pressure, you need lateral.
Shoulders and hips perpendicular to bed, with the plane of the back vertical rather than rolled
Once the needle is in and before measuring, let the legs come down. Flexion falsely raises the opening pressure.
steps: Suspected meningitis: blood cultures, then antibiotics, then everything below.
Review contraindications and the imaging criteria, consent, and required studies.
Position patient carefully, identify the interspace, and mark it.
Prep/drape sterile field.
Anesthetize skin and deeper tissue.
Insert the introducer, then the atraumatic needle through it, angled slightly cephalad. Bevel orientation is a cutting-needle instruction and does not apply to a pencil-point needle.
Advance slowly. An atraumatic needle gives a subtle or absent pop, so check for flow every few millimetres by removing the stylet rather than waiting for a feel that may never come.
Measure opening pressure before removing any CSF: lateral position, legs and neck relaxed, manometer zeroed at the interspace.
Collect CSF in ordered tubes.
Replace stylet before removing needle; dress site and reassess the neurological examination.
ultrasound: Ultrasound can help identify midline and depth in obese or difficult anatomy but does not replace sterile technique.
It is most useful before the first attempt, as a marking tool, rather than after three failures.
confirmation: CSF obtained and sent for ordered studies

Opening pressure measured before CSF removal, with the position, leg position, and zero reference recorded beside the number. A commonly cited adult range is about 6-25 cmH2O, and a number recorded without its conditions is not interpretable.
Straining, coughing, Valsalva, hypercapnia, and a flexed position all raise it. A single high number in a struggling patient is not intracranial hypertension.
Patient neurologic status reassessed
Tube numbers and appearance documented
troubleshooting: No CSF: recheck positioning, level, angle, depth; consider longer needle or ultrasound marking.
Bone repeatedly: withdraw to subcutaneous tissue and redirect cephalad slightly.
Flow starts then stops: rotate the needle 90 degrees. A nerve root or the arachnoid can occlude the aperture, and rotating is gentler than advancing.
Traumatic tap: minimize needle movement; consider another level if needed.
Post-LP headache: counsel, fluids/analgesia, blood patch pathway if persistent/severe.
complications: Spinal or epidural haematoma - rare, and the reason the anticoagulation question is not a formality
aftercare: Bed rest does not prevent post-dural-puncture headache. Lying flat may make an established one more tolerable; do not offer it as prophylaxis.
Send CSF promptly with correct labels and orders.
Reassess neuro status and puncture site.

New or worsening back pain, leg weakness, numbness, or urinary retention after an LP is a spinal or epidural haematoma until proven otherwise. Urgent MRI and a neurosurgical conversation - not analgesia and reassurance. The risk is highest in anticoagulated or coagulopathic patients, and the window in which decompression preserves function is hours.
Give return precautions for severe headache, fever, weakness, urinary retention, or site issues.
documentation: Lumbar puncture performed for documented indication.
Consent obtained; contraindications and imaging criteria reviewed as appropriate.
Where meningitis was suspected: time of blood cultures, time of first antibiotic dose, and time of LP, so the order is on the record.
Patient positioned and sterile technique used.
Needle type and gauge documented - atraumatic or cutting - and the level of insertion.
CSF obtained or unsuccessful attempts documented.
Opening pressure documented with position, leg position, and zero reference if measured.
CSF appearance/tubes/studies documented; patient tolerated procedure with complications noted.
seniorPearls: Most failed LPs are positioning failures, not needle failures.
Do not chase bone deeper and deeper; reset your angle.
Label tubes before you are holding CSF and everyone is suddenly excited.
The atraumatic needle has no satisfying pop. Check for flow instead of waiting for a feeling.
If you are about to delay antibiotics for the LP, the order of this procedure is backwards.

Engelborghs S, et al. Consensus guidelines for lumbar puncture in patients with neurological diseases. Alzheimers Dement (Amst). 2017;8:111-126. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5454085/
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Injection safety and lumbar puncture infection-control practices. https://www.cdc.gov/injection-safety/hcp/clinical-guidance/index.html

Link the local antithrombotic policy that governs hold intervals before neuraxial puncture. ASRA Pain Medicine's fifth-edition guideline is the usual source document for that policy: https://doi.org/10.1136/rapm-2024-105766
Verify local institutional policy, kit contents, consent requirements, and credentialing expectations.

visualAssets.title: LP interspace landmarks
visualAssets.subtitle: Tuffier's line (a line connecting the iliac crests) crosses at approximately the L4 spinous process. L3–L4 or L4–L5 interspaces are the target, below the conus medullaris.
visualAssets.caption: Illustration pending clinical review. Use the visual asset workflow before bundling final artwork.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: The conus medullaris typically ends at L1–L2. Do not insert above L3.

visualAssets.title: Needle trajectory
visualAssets.subtitle: Midline approach: needle angled slightly cephalad, passing through skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, then dura. Pop felt at dura entry.
visualAssets.caption: Replace assetName with reviewed artwork when available.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: If bone is hit, withdraw and redirect — do not force through.

agents.note: Epinephrine buys a higher ceiling and a drier field. Avoid it in an end-arterial field unless local policy says otherwise.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than lidocaine or ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Toxicity adds up, but the maximums are not interchangeable and two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling and keep the fractions adding to less than one - half the lidocaine maximum plus half the bupivacaine maximum is a full dose, not half of one. Everything counts: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

Where it goes changes how fast it arrives. The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, designated by the clinical owner. The drug labels do not publish one universal figure per agent: they require individualisation by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary and is not the same as being safe.

shiftMode: Confirm indication, site preference (radial first), and assess collateral flow with ultrasound before committing.
Position wrist in 20-30° extension over a firm roll; tape securely without restricting distal circulation.
Ultrasound preferred: identify radial artery, confirm pulsatility and depth, plan entry point.
Anesthetize even in awake patients — arterial puncture without local anesthetic causes involuntary movement and failed placement.
Advance catheter-over-needle with bevel up at 30-45°; on flashback, flatten and advance catheter. Use Seldinger for deep or small vessels.
Arterial waveform on the transducer is definitive confirmation — a flat or venous tracing means reposition or replace.
Label, zero at the phlebostatic axis, and square-wave test before relying on readings. Re-level after every bed height change.
MAP is relatively protected when the trace is damped or resonant; the systolic is not. Titrate to MAP.
indications: Continuous beat-to-beat blood pressure monitoring in hemodynamic instability or vasopressor titration
Frequent arterial blood gas sampling (>4-6 ABGs anticipated)
Non-invasive BP unreliable due to arrhythmia, severe hypotension, obesity, or peripheral vascular disease
High-risk procedures, RSI, or sedation requiring real-time hemodynamic monitoring
contraindications: No identifiable arterial signal at planned site — do not attempt blind
Raynaud phenomenon, limb ischemia, or insufficient collateral flow (relative; assess with ultrasound)
Active infection, burn, or wound overlying the insertion site
Suspected arterial disease, thrombosis, or prior catheterization damage at site
Severe coagulopathy — weigh urgency; compressible sites preferred
anatomy: Radial artery runs along the lateral volar forearm, superficial to the flexor carpi radialis tendon; typically 2-4 mm diameter at 3-8 mm depth.
Dual radial-ulnar supply provides collateral protection; assess with ultrasound if perfusion uncertain.
Femoral offers larger target but higher infection and noncompressible-bleeding risk.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial are alternatives when upper extremities are inaccessible.
Artery is pulsatile and non-compressible; distinguish clearly from the adjacent cephalic vein.
equipment: Arterial catheter kit or 20-gauge catheter-over-needle with Seldinger wire
Alcoholic chlorhexidine over 0.5% (alternative agent if contraindicated)
Cap, mask, sterile gloves, and a sterile fenestrated drape; full maximal barriers for femoral or axillary placement
Local anesthetic (1% lidocaine), syringe, and small-gauge needle
Arm board or rolled towel for wrist positioning
Tape for securement
Arterial pressure transducer and tubing with NS flush bag pressurized to 300 mmHg
Ultrasound machine with sterile probe cover and sterile gel
Clear occlusive dressing
Suture or adhesive securement device per preference
Monitor with arterial waveform capability
positioning: Extend wrist 20-30° over a firm roll (rolled towel or IV bag) with the volar surface facing up.
Tape hand and forearm securely to arm board; prevent movement without restricting distal perfusion.
Abduct arm and position ultrasound screen in direct line of sight before prep.
steps: Confirm indication, check for contraindications, and obtain consent if non-emergent.
Set up pressure transducer and tubing; connect to monitor and zero at the phlebostatic axis.
Position wrist over roll in 20-30° extension; secure with tape.
Perform ultrasound survey: identify artery, confirm pulsatility, estimate depth, and plan entry point.
Prep skin widely with chlorhexidine; apply sterile drape.
Infiltrate skin and subcutaneous tissue with local anesthetic along the planned tract.
With ultrasound guidance, advance needle at 30-45° bevel-up; watch for pulsatile flash.

On flash: for catheter-over-needle, flatten slightly, advance catheter off needle, remove needle; for Seldinger, flatten, pass wire without force, remove needle, thread catheter over wire, remove wire.
Connect arterial tubing; confirm arterial waveform on monitor.
Secure catheter, apply clear dressing, and label with site and date.

Perform a square-wave (fast-flush) test before treating any displayed number: one to two oscillations back to baseline is adequate; more than two with sharp overshoot is underdamped and reads systolic too high; a slurred return with no oscillation is overdamped and reads systolic too low.
Until the trace passes that test, titrate vasoactives to MAP rather than systolic and correlate against a cuff.
ultrasound: Short-axis approach: confirm artery is pulsatile and non-compressible; distinguish from adjacent vein.
Long-axis approach: useful for visualizing needle trajectory and catheter advancement.
Confirm wire position in vessel lumen before advancing catheter with Seldinger technique.
Post-placement: assess distal perfusion if any concern about thrombosis or vasospasm.
confirmation: Pulsatile arterial waveform visible on bedside monitor
Bright red flash at time of needle entry
Catheter flushes smoothly with no resistance
Catheter secured and labeled; transducer zeroed
Square-wave test performed and the trace judged adequately damped
Flush system continuously pressurized at ~300 mmHg
troubleshooting: Flash without waveform: check transducer connections, tubing, and zero; re-advance catheter slightly or retry Seldinger.
Catheter will not advance over needle: do not force; switch to Seldinger technique or resite.

Overdamped (slurred square-wave return, systolic reads low): hunt air bubbles in the tubing and transducer first, then tip clot, kink, loose connection, flush bag below 300 mmHg, or over-long compliant tubing.

Underdamped or resonant (more than two oscillations, systolic reads high by 20-30 mmHg): shorten the circuit, remove unnecessary stopcocks, consider a damping device. Expect it in tachycardic, hyperdynamic patients.
Displayed pressure does not fit the patient: re-level at the phlebostatic axis, repeat the square-wave test, and compare with a cuff. A transducer 10 cm off is about 7.5 mmHg of error.
Loss of signal with movement: improve limb securement and confirm catheter is not kinked.
Hematoma: remove catheter, hold firm pressure ≥5 min (longer if anticoagulated), and check distal perfusion.
complications: Thrombosis with distal ischemia — remove catheter immediately if suspected
Infection - risk rises with femoral site, longer dwell, and emergent insertion, not with a fixed number of hours
aftercare: Remove catheter as soon as hemodynamic monitoring is no longer required.
Hold firm pressure 5-10 minutes after removal (longer if anticoagulated).
Assess distal perfusion and capillary refill after removal.

Do not resite on a schedule. Replace only for a clinical indication - local or systemic infection, malfunction, or distal ischemia. Prompt removal when monitoring is no longer needed is the only measure that reliably lowers infection.
documentation: Arterial line placed at [radial/femoral/dorsalis pedis] for [indication].
Consent obtained when feasible; emergent need documented when not possible.
Ultrasound guidance used; vessel confirmed as artery by pulsatility and non-compressibility.
Catheter advanced via [catheter-over-needle / Seldinger] technique.
Arterial waveform confirmed on monitor; transducer zeroed.
Catheter secured with clear dressing and labeled with date and site.
Distal perfusion intact after placement.
seniorPearls: The wrist roll is often underdone — a firm, secure 20-30° extension dramatically improves first-pass success.
Seldinger technique outperforms catheter-over-needle in patients with deep, small, or difficult vessels.

A persistently dampened waveform is a reason to fix or replace the line, not to accept inaccurate readings - and underdamping is the more dangerous direction, because it hides hypotension behind a falsely reassuring systolic.
references: CDC. Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections: arterial catheters and pressure-monitoring systems. 2011 guideline, page updated 2024. https://www.cdc.gov/infection-control/hcp/intravascular-catheter-related-infections/summary-recommendations.html

Saugel B, Kouz K, Meidert AS, Schulte-Uentrop L, Romagnoli S. How to measure blood pressure using an arterial catheter: a systematic 5-step approach. Crit Care. 2020;24(1):172. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32331527/
Romagnoli S et al. Accuracy of invasive arterial pressure monitoring in cardiovascular patients: an observational study. Crit Care. 2014;18(6):644. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25433536/

visualAssets.title: Radial artery approach
visualAssets.subtitle: Wrist extended 30–45 degrees over a towel roll. Radial artery palpated 1–2 cm proximal to the wrist crease, lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon.
visualAssets.caption: Replace assetName with reviewed artwork when available.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Avoid hyperextension — it can occlude the artery.

visualAssets.title: Ultrasound short-axis view
visualAssets.subtitle: Linear probe perpendicular to the radial artery. Small pulsatile structure visible at 2–5 mm depth. Radial nerve and vein are adjacent.
visualAssets.caption: Replace assetName with reviewed artwork when available.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Use minimal probe pressure to avoid compressing the artery flat.

shiftMode: Confirm indication (diagnostic vs. therapeutic) and laterality; verify effusion is free-flowing on ultrasound — not loculated.
Mark the site with the patient in the procedure position; fluid pockets shift significantly when patients change position.

Puncture over the superior margin of the lower rib. The intercostal bundle runs vein-artery-nerve from superior to inferior in the costal groove, and it is not reliably tucked under the rib - collateral branches can sit mid-space.
Anesthetize all the way to the pleural surface — the parietal pleura is where the pain is.

For therapeutic: connect drainage before advancing the catheter; preventing air entry is critical. Manual syringe aspiration or gravity to a bag below the patient - never a vacuum bottle or wall suction.

Drain to symptoms, not to a number. Stop and clamp - not merely slow - for repetitive cough, chest tightness or pain, or worsening breathlessness; these precede re-expansion pulmonary oedema. General ceiling is 1.5 L in one session.

Check lung sliding on ultrasound immediately in everyone. Chest x-ray only if symptomatic, air was aspirated, the procedure was difficult, sliding is absent or uncertain, or the patient is ventilated or cannot report symptoms.
Adult scope only. Paediatric site selection, device size, and dosing differ materially and are not covered by this card.
indications: Diagnostic evaluation of a new, undiagnosed pleural effusion
Therapeutic relief of respiratory compromise from a large pleural effusion
Evaluation of parapneumonic effusion for empyema, complicated effusion, or effusion requiring drainage
contraindications: Uncooperative patient unable to remain still during procedure (relative; consider procedural sedation)
Uncorrected coagulopathy with significant bleeding risk — weigh urgency and available reversal
Effusion too small or clearly loculated with no safe accessible pocket on ultrasound
Pneumothorax with effusion, or hydropneumothorax, is a chest-tube problem rather than a thoracentesis problem
Known lung adherence to chest wall at the planned site
Adult scope only. Paediatric site selection, device size, and dosing differ materially and are not covered by this card.
anatomy: Pleural space lies between parietal and visceral pleura; fluid accumulates in dependent regions (posterior on upright imaging).

Intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove of each rib in the order vein, artery, nerve from superior to inferior; puncture over the superior margin of the lower rib. The bundle is not reliably protected by the rib - it varies in position, particularly posteriorly, and collateral branches can lie mid-space, so stay as lateral or anterior as the target allows.
Diaphragm rises during expiration and varies with body habitus; ultrasound confirms safe distance before puncture.
Right-sided approach: liver is at risk below the 9th rib posteriorly.
Left-sided approach: spleen is at risk; confirm upper boundary of effusion before each approach.
equipment: Thoracentesis kit (needle, catheter, three-way stopcock, 60 mL syringe)
Ultrasound machine
Chlorhexidine prep
Sterile drape, sterile gloves, mask
Local anesthetic (1% lidocaine), syringe, and 22-25 gauge anesthesia needle
Drainage tubing with a three-way stopcock for manual syringe aspiration, or a gravity bag hung below the patient. Vacuum bottles and wall suction are not used for therapeutic aspiration.
Plain specimen containers for LDH, protein, glucose, cell count with differential, Gram stain, culture, and cytology as appropriate
Blood culture bottles inoculated at the bedside in addition to plain containers when pleural infection is suspected - both, not blood cultures alone
Heparinised blood-gas syringe for pleural pH, analysed immediately on a gas analyser
Occlusive dressing
Drainage measurement container
positioning: Seated and leaning forward over a padded bedside table with arms resting on a pillow — drops the scapula and opens interspaces for posterior access.
Supine with ipsilateral arm raised overhead is acceptable for ventilated or unable-to-sit patients; locate fluid in this position.
Perform ultrasound with the patient in the exact position you will use for the procedure.
steps: Confirm the effusion side, size, and indication; determine diagnostic vs. therapeutic approach.
Obtain consent when feasible; document emergent need if not possible.
Perform real-time ultrasound with patient in procedure position; identify the optimal fluid pocket and mark the entry site.
Prep and drape the posterior-lateral chest at the marked site.

Anesthetize skin, subcutaneous tissue, rib periosteum, and pleural surface to the weight-based ceiling on the max-dose card, aspirating as you advance. Keep lidocaine out of any sample destined for pH.
Insert the procedure needle along the superior margin of the lower rib with continuous aspiration.
On pleural fluid return, lock needle position; for diagnostic aspiration, collect 30-60 mL directly.
For therapeutic: advance catheter over needle or via Seldinger technique, then connect drainage tubing to prevent air entry.
Drain by manual syringe aspiration through the stopcock, or by gravity to a bag below the patient. Monitor symptoms continuously.

Drain to symptoms, not to a number. Stop and clamp - not merely slow - for repetitive cough, chest tightness or pain, or worsening breathlessness; these precede re-expansion pulmonary oedema. General ceiling is 1.5 L in one session.
Withdraw catheter/needle at end of expiration or with patient performing Valsalva; apply occlusive dressing immediately.
Check lung sliding on ultrasound immediately. Obtain a chest x-ray only on the selective criteria, not routinely.
ultrasound: Use a low-frequency curvilinear or phased-array probe in the posterior-lateral chest to identify the effusion in coronal plane.
Confirm fluid is anechoic or hypoechoic and free-flowing with respiration — loculations appear as hyperechoic strands.
Measure the largest pocket depth and distance from skin to fluid before marking.
Mark the entry site with the patient in the procedure position; fluid pockets shift with position changes.
Post-procedure: scan for pneumothorax (absent lung sliding ipsilateral) before imaging is complete.
confirmation: Pleural fluid aspirated freely and consistent with expected character (serous, serosanguineous, or purulent)
No sudden air return (would indicate lung puncture or pneumothorax development)
Respiratory symptoms improved for therapeutic indication
Lung sliding present on immediate post-procedure ultrasound; chest x-ray reserved for the selective criteria
Specimens labeled and sent promptly
troubleshooting: No fluid on aspiration: confirm with real-time ultrasound — pocket may have shifted; use live guidance for next attempt.
Air return: withdraw immediately; the needle may be in lung parenchyma; assess urgently for pneumothorax.
Bloody return: distinguish hemorrhagic effusion from hemothorax vs. vessel injury — non-clotting blood suggests pleural; rapidly clotting suggests vascular.

Drain to symptoms, not to a number. Stop and clamp - not merely slow - for repetitive cough, chest tightness or pain, or worsening breathlessness; these precede re-expansion pulmonary oedema. General ceiling is 1.5 L in one session.
Loculated pocket: scan multiple windows; if truly inaccessible, consult interventional radiology or thoracics.
complications: Pneumothorax - uncommon, and substantially less likely with ultrasound guidance than without
aftercare: Monitor O2 saturation, respiratory rate, and breath sounds for ≥1 hour after procedure.
Immediate lung ultrasound for sliding in everyone; chest x-ray only on the selective criteria.

Send samples promptly. Pleural pH goes in a heparinised blood-gas syringe and is analysed immediately: lidocaine contamination and excess heparin both falsely lower it, and pH below 7.2 is what drives the decision to drain. Do not send pH on frank pus - drain it regardless, and it fouls the analyser. A dipstick or benchtop meter is not accurate enough for this decision.
Record total volume drained and fluid character; document in procedure note.
documentation: Thoracentesis performed at [right/left], [interspace], for [indication].
Consent obtained / emergent need documented.
Ultrasound guidance used for site selection and real-time guidance.
[Volume] mL of [serous/serosanguineous/purulent] fluid drained; no air return.
Specimens sent for [LDH, protein, cell count, culture, cytology as ordered].
Post-procedure imaging: [result, e.g., no pneumothorax, residual small effusion].
Patient tolerated procedure without oxygen desaturation, respiratory distress, or significant bleeding.
seniorPearls: Mark the site with the patient in the procedure position — the fluid pocket moves when they lie down and you will miss it.

Most missed pneumothoraces are in ventilated or obtunded patients who cannot report symptoms. That is exactly the group to image liberally, and the reason the awake asymptomatic patient with good sliding does not need a film.
Stop before 1.5 L unless you have a compelling reason and are monitoring closely; re-expansion pulmonary edema is rare but underappreciated.

shiftMode: Confirm indication (diagnostic vs. therapeutic); verify ascites is present and accessible by ultrasound.
Ultrasound marks the largest, safest pocket in the LLQ - avoids bowel, bladder, and inferior epigastric vessels.
Z-track technique: displace skin laterally before needle entry, release after entering peritoneum - reduces post-procedure fluid leak.
For large-volume (>5 L): administer albumin 6-8 g per litre removed to prevent paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunction.

Below 5 L albumin is not routine, but it is not forbidden either. Acute-on-chronic liver failure or a high risk of post-paracentesis acute kidney injury are reasons to give it at a smaller volume - a judgement, not a threshold.
Every hospitalized cirrhotic with ascites who decompensates needs a diagnostic tap - you cannot rule out SBP clinically.
Inoculate blood culture bottles at the bedside from the first 10-20 mL drawn - highest diagnostic yield for SBP.
Do not delay or cancel the tap to correct clotting numbers. Routine coagulation testing and prophylactic products are not recommended before paracentesis.
indications: New-onset ascites requiring diagnostic evaluation
Suspected spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in any hospitalized patient with cirrhosis and ascites
Therapeutic large-volume paracentesis for tense or symptomatic ascites causing respiratory compromise or discomfort
Evaluation of ascites in acute decompensated liver disease, malignancy, or unknown etiology
contraindications: Disseminated intravascular coagulation or clinically active bleeding - the one coagulopathy that genuinely changes the decision
Surgical abdomen where bowel perforation is possible at all accessible sites
Active infection, wound, or burn overlying all potential insertion sites
Known adhesions or bowel loops adherent to the anterior abdominal wall at the planned site

There is no INR or platelet threshold on this card, and the earlier INR >2.0 and platelets <50,000 gates were removed. Current cirrhosis guidance recommends against routine coagulation testing and against prophylactic plasma or platelets before paracentesis, because the INR does not describe bleeding risk in cirrhosis. Assess bleeding risk clinically and follow local procedural policy.
anatomy: Standard entry: LLQ 4-6 cm lateral to the midline, midway between umbilicus and anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS).
RLQ is acceptable alternative if LLQ is unsafe due to prior surgery, ostomy, or other anatomy.
Avoid the midline: risk of diastasis, recanalized umbilical vein, and thin soft tissue.
Inferior epigastric vessels run cephalocaudally approximately 3-5 cm medial to the ASIS — confirm with Doppler ultrasound.
The bladder must be empty; the bowel shifts unpredictably. Ultrasound-guided entry is standard of care.
equipment: Paracentesis kit or 18-gauge needle/catheter with three-way stopcock and 60 mL syringe (diagnostic)
Long catheter or pigtail drain for therapeutic drainage >1 L
Ultrasound machine
Chlorhexidine prep
Sterile drape, sterile gloves
Local anesthetic: 1% lidocaine, syringe, and small-gauge needle
Large-bore drainage tubing and collection containers for therapeutic tap
Specimen tubes for cell count with differential, ascitic albumin, protein, LDH, glucose, and culture

A paired serum albumin drawn at the same time. The serum-ascites albumin gradient needs both halves, and a lone ascitic albumin cannot be interpreted - order it with the tap for any new or undifferentiated ascites.
Blood culture bottles for bedside inoculation (best yield for SBP detection)
Occlusive dressing or small bandage
positioning: Supine with slight left lateral decubitus (left side down) to pool ascites in the LLQ.
Head of bed elevated 30° if patient cannot lie flat due to respiratory compromise.
Empty the bladder before starting — foley or void — to clear the pelvic space.
Scan with the patient in the exact position you will use for the procedure.
steps: Confirm indication and approach (diagnostic vs. therapeutic); verify ascites on ultrasound.
Empty bladder; position patient in slight left lateral decubitus.
Obtain consent when feasible; document emergent need when not possible.
Perform real-time ultrasound; identify optimal pocket in the LLQ or RLQ; mark the entry site.
Prep and drape the marked area.
Anesthetize skin, subcutaneous tissue, and peritoneum with local anesthetic, aspirating as you advance to confirm proximity to fluid.
Using Z-track technique (displace skin 1-2 cm laterally before advancing; release after entering peritoneum), insert needle perpendicular to skin with continuous aspiration.
On peritoneal fluid return, lock needle or advance catheter; note character of fluid.
Diagnostic: collect 30-60 mL, inoculate blood culture bottles at the bedside, and send the labelled specimens with a paired serum albumin.
Therapeutic: connect drainage tubing to catheter; allow gravity or low-pressure drainage.

Over 5 L: give albumin at 6-8 g per litre removed, during or immediately after drainage. Under 5 L: give it if this patient has acute-on-chronic liver failure or a high risk of acute kidney injury, and record the reason either way.
Withdraw needle/catheter when drainage complete; apply firm pressure briefly; dress the site with an occlusive bandage.
Monitor BP, HR, and symptoms for 30-60 minutes post-procedure.
ultrasound: Use a curvilinear or low-frequency probe to identify the largest free-flowing fluid pocket in the LLQ.
Confirm depth from skin to fluid and the absence of bowel loops in the intended needle path.
Color Doppler at the planned site identifies the inferior epigastric vessels before puncture.
Mark the entry site with the patient in the procedure position — fluid redistributes when position changes.
Post-procedure: brief scan to assess for residual ascites and any hematoma at the entry site.
confirmation: Peritoneal fluid returns freely on aspiration - straw-colored, turbid, milky, or bloody depending on etiology
Fluid flows freely during therapeutic drainage
No bowel contents (feculent material or food particles) in return
Abdominal distension and discomfort reduce during therapeutic drainage
Albumin decision made and recorded - given with the volume and dose, or withheld with the reason
troubleshooting: No fluid return: confirm position with ultrasound; needle may have bypassed the pocket; withdraw and reassess live.
Bowel contents in return: withdraw immediately; monitor for peritonitis signs; most isolated needle punctures of bowel are self-limiting.
Catheter clogs during large-volume tap: reposition patient slightly; flush gently; replace if blocked.
Persistent fluid leak from site post-procedure: hold pressure; Z-track technique reduces this; purse-string suture rarely required.
Neutrophils >250/mm³ with SBP suspicion: treat empirically while awaiting confirmatory culture results.
complications: Paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunction (large volume without albumin replacement)
Persistent ascites leak requiring surgical repair (rare)
aftercare: Albumin: confirm it was given for volumes above 5 L, and that the below-5-L decision was made rather than defaulted. Reassess BP and HR at 1 hour.
Check renal function and electrolytes after a large-volume tap in anyone with acute-on-chronic liver failure, baseline renal impairment, or hypotension during drainage.
Send specimens promptly; a neutrophil count above 250 cells/mm3 meets criteria for empiric SBP treatment.
Monitor for abdominal pain, fever, or hematoma for 4-6 hours after the procedure.
Record total volume drained and fluid character in the procedure note.
Educate patient on return precautions: worsening pain, fever, spreading redness, or fluid leak from the site.
documentation: Paracentesis performed at [LLQ/RLQ] for [indication].
Consent obtained / emergent need documented.
Ultrasound guidance used; largest pocket identified at [site].
[Volume] mL of [character] peritoneal fluid removed without complication.
Specimens sent for [cell count, albumin, protein, LDH, culture, cytology as ordered]; blood culture bottles inoculated at bedside.
Albumin [administered at X g per liter / not indicated — volume <5 L].
Patient hemodynamically stable post-procedure; no abdominal rigidity or signs of peritonitis.
seniorPearls: Every hospitalized cirrhotic who decompensates gets a diagnostic tap first - you cannot exclude SBP on exam.
The INR in cirrhosis is not a bleeding-risk score. Waiting on plasma delays a tap that diagnoses the thing killing the patient.
Order the serum albumin with the tap. A gradient needs two numbers and the second one is the one people forget.
The Z-track technique reduces post-tap ascites leak; teach it and use it consistently.
Albumin replacement for large-volume taps is not optional; paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunction is underdiagnosed and preventable.
references: European Association for the Study of the Liver. EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines for the management of patients with decompensated cirrhosis. J Hepatol. 2018;69(2):406-460. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhep.2018.03.024

American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases. Diagnosis, Evaluation, and Management of Ascites, Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis and Hepatorenal Syndrome. https://www.aasld.org/practice-guidelines/diagnosis-evaluation-and-management-ascites-spontaneous-bacterial-peritonitis

Aithal GP, et al. Guidelines on the management of ascites in cirrhosis. British Society of Gastroenterology and British Association for the Study of the Liver. Gut. 2021;70(1):9-29. https://doi.org/10.1136/gutjnl-2020-321790
Verify local procedural policy on periprocedural coagulation assessment and the albumin preparation stocked.

agents.note: Epinephrine buys a higher ceiling and a drier field. Avoid it in an end-arterial field unless local policy says otherwise.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than lidocaine or ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Toxicity adds up, but the maximums are not interchangeable and two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling and keep the fractions adding to less than one - half the lidocaine maximum plus half the bupivacaine maximum is a full dose, not half of one. Everything counts: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

Where it goes changes how fast it arrives. The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, designated by the clinical owner. The drug labels do not publish one universal figure per agent: they require individualisation by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary and is not the same as being safe.

shiftMode: Confirm this is a fluctuant abscess, not cellulitis, a lipoma, or a lymph node - ultrasound identifies occult pockets and depth, avoids dry incisions.
Anesthetize generously before incising - acidic pus inactivates local anesthetic near the core; infiltrate widely around the margin and wait.
The incision must be adequate: span the entire fluctuant cavity and allow complete drainage and loculation breakdown.

Drainage and breaking down loculations is the treatment. Irrigation is optional - a randomised trial found no improvement in outcome from routine cavity irrigation, and it adds pain, time, and splash exposure. Irrigate a grossly contaminated or debris-filled cavity, and skip it for a clean one.

Packing is also not routine. For a simple abscess under about 5 cm, routine packing added pain without reducing reintervention. Leave it open, or use a loop drain where the cavity or the site makes premature closure likely.
Primary closure is contraindicated - leave it open.
Antibiotics are a shared decision rather than a reflex in either direction. See aftercare.
indications: Fluctuant, loculated skin or soft tissue abscess confirmed clinically or by ultrasound
Infected sebaceous cyst, pilonidal abscess, or other skin abscess requiring drainage
Paronychia with subungual extension unresponsive to soaking
contraindications: Tissue not clearly fluctuant and abscess not confirmed — do not incise cellulitis blindly
Hand deep-space infection (flexor tenosynovitis risk) — surgical consultation required
Facial abscess near the dangerous triangle or other high-risk vascular territory — surgical consultation preferred
Signs of necrotizing infection (pain out of proportion, crepitus, skin necrosis, rapid spread) — this is a surgical emergency, not a bedside I&D
Abscess adjacent to neurovascular structures or deep fascia without adequate training and imaging
anatomy: Identify abscess boundaries by palpation and ultrasound; plan incision at point of maximal fluctuance.
Avoid crossing joint lines, tendon sheaths, or neurovascular structures with the incision when possible.
Satellite collections are common — explore for and break down connecting loculations with blunt dissection.
Perirectal and ischiorectal abscesses require colorectal or surgical expertise; do not attempt without proper training.
Avoid end-arterial zones (fingertip, toe, pinna, nasal tip, penis) with epinephrine-containing anesthetic.
equipment: Scalpel with #11 or #15 blade
Iris scissors and curved hemostat for blunt dissection
Irrigation syringe and normal saline, if irrigating - not a fixed volume, and not for every cavity
Splash guard or angiocatheter tip for directed irrigation
Loop drain (Penrose or vessel loop) or plain strip gauze packing, for the cavities that need one
Sterile gloves and sterile drape
Chlorhexidine or betadine prep
Local anesthetic: 1% lidocaine with epinephrine (avoid end-arterial zones) or regional block
Non-adherent wound dressing and tape
Wound cultures if immunocompromise, recurrence, or systemic infection suspected
positioning: Position the abscess for optimal visualization and operator ergonomics — often lateral decubitus for buttock or perianal.
Adequate lighting is critical; use a headlamp or task light for depth visualization.
Pediatric patients may require restraint assistance or procedural sedation for larger abscesses.
steps: Confirm diagnosis with exam and ultrasound; identify all pockets, satellite collections, and the point of maximal fluctuance.
Infiltrate local anesthetic widely around and beneath the abscess margin - not into the cavity. Allow adequate time for onset (2-3 minutes minimum).
Optionally consider regional nerve block for large or anatomically favorable abscesses.
Prep the area; apply sterile drape.
Make a single, adequate linear incision through the abscess dome at maximal fluctuance - it must be long enough to allow complete drainage and instrument access.
Gently express contents; do not squeeze forcefully.
Insert closed hemostat, open along cavity axis, and sweep to break down all loculations - confirm cavity extent. This is the step that treats the abscess.
Irrigate if the cavity is grossly contaminated or full of debris. There is no evidence-based volume and no requirement to irrigate until the return runs clear.

Decide on a drain: a simple cavity under about 5 cm in an otherwise well patient can be left open with no packing. Use a loop drain for larger or deeper cavities, or where the skin will close over the space before it fills in. If you pack, pack loosely - packing is a spacer, not a treatment.
Apply non-adherent dressing.
Plan follow-up at 48-72 hours for drain assessment or wound check.
ultrasound: High-frequency linear probe (10+ MHz) for soft tissue abscess identification.
Confirms hypoechoic or anechoic fluid cavity with posterior acoustic enhancement and internal debris — differentiates from solid mass.
Color Doppler identifies adjacent vessels before incision.
Reveals hidden loculations and satellite pockets that palpation alone misses.
Use ultrasound to guide needle aspiration for depth confirmation before incision in deep or uncertain abscesses.
confirmation: Frank pus drains freely on incision
All loculations broken down and cavity fully explored with instrument
Cavity left open, or a loop drain or loose packing placed where indicated - not tight, not obliterating the cavity
No evidence of deeper structure involvement (tendon, joint, fascia)
troubleshooting: No pus on incision: reassess with ultrasound — may have incised into cellulitis or missed the pocket; do not extend blindly.
Bleeding during incision: direct pressure; abscess-bed bleeding is usually minor and self-limited.
Inadequate anesthesia despite infiltration: add more anesthetic outside the margin, wait longer; acidic purulent environment inactivates local anesthetic near the core.
Deep pocket inaccessible: ultrasound-guided aspiration to confirm location; surgical consultation if complex anatomy or uncertain.
Recurrence at same site: consider incomplete drainage, retained foreign body, hidradenitis suppurativa, Crohn's disease, or resistant organism.
complications: Abscess recurrence from inadequate drainage or premature closure
Bacteremia (rare with simple abscess; consider antibiotics if systemic signs develop)
Injury to adjacent neurovascular structures if anatomy is not respected
aftercare: Instruct patient on wound care: warm soaks or showering; keep the site clean and moist.
Return visit in 48-72 hours for drain assessment and wound inspection.

Antibiotics are a conversation, not a default. Drainage alone cures most simple abscesses, and adding trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or clindamycin produces a modest reduction in treatment failure and recurrence at the cost of adverse effects - enough for a weak, shared-decision recommendation rather than a rule. Antibiotics are clearly indicated for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, immunocompromise, a facial or hand location, or a prosthesis nearby.
Where antibiotics are given, choose against local resistance patterns and cover MRSA where prevalence warrants it.
Provide clear return precautions: worsening pain, fever, spreading redness, or red streaking.
documentation: Abscess incision and drainage performed at [site and description] for [indication].
Ultrasound performed: [confirmed abscess / depth / satellite collections noted].
Local anesthetic with [agent/concentration] administered; patient reported adequate analgesia.
[Character and estimated volume of pus] evacuated; cavity irrigated with normal saline until clear.
Loculations broken down; [loop drain / loose packing] placed.
Cultures [sent / not sent]; antibiotics [prescribed / not prescribed] with rationale documented.
Patient discharged with wound care instructions and 48-72 hour follow-up arranged.
seniorPearls: Acidic pus inactivates local anesthetic inside the cavity - infiltrate around the margin and wait; never rush into an under-anesthetized abscess.
The incision length is the most common technical mistake: if you cannot freely break down all loculations, it is not big enough.
Breaking down loculations is the therapy. Irrigation and packing are both optional extras that the evidence has been unkind to.
Packing a small simple abscess makes the follow-up visit worse and the outcome no better.
references: Stevens DL, et al. Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Skin and Soft Tissue Infections: 2014 Update by IDSA. Clin Infect Dis. 2014;59(2):e10-e52. https://doi.org/10.1093/cid/ciu296
Chinnock B, Hendey GW. Irrigation of cutaneous abscesses does not improve treatment success. Ann Emerg Med. 2016;67(3):379-383. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.annemergmed.2015.08.007
O'Malley GF, et al. Routine packing of simple cutaneous abscesses is painful and probably unnecessary. Acad Emerg Med. 2009;16(5):470-473. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1553-2712.2009.00409.x
Vermandere M, et al. Antibiotics after incision and drainage for uncomplicated skin abscesses: a clinical practice guideline. BMJ. 2018;360:k243. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.k243
Talan DA, et al. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole versus placebo for uncomplicated skin abscess. N Engl J Med. 2016;374(9):823-832. https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1507476

shiftMode: Confirm you actually need large-bore central access (massive transfusion, rapid volume, or a conduit for a transvenous pacer/PA catheter) — a triple lumen is not interchangeable with an introducer.
Full sterile barrier and ultrasound, exactly as for any central line. The larger dilator is less forgiving, not more.
Confirm the wire is venous before dilating — arterial dilation with an 8.5 Fr sheath is a surgical emergency.
Dilator and sheath advance together as a unit over the wire; keep the wire moving freely and never lose the back end.
Advance with gentle rotation, not force. The skin nick must be adequate or the sheath tip will peel back.
Remove dilator and wire together, then immediately cap or connect the side port and aspirate/flush.
Confirm position and screen for pneumothorax/arterial placement per site and local policy.
indications: Anticipated massive transfusion or rapid large-volume resuscitation
Need for a conduit to float a transvenous pacemaker or pulmonary artery catheter
High-flow access when peripheral large-bore IVs are inadequate or impossible
Hemodynamic instability requiring reliable, high-flow central access
contraindications: Patient refusal when non-emergent
Infection, burn, or significant injury overlying the intended site
Thrombosis or distorted anatomy at the intended vein
Uncorrected severe coagulopathy is a relative risk; weigh against urgency and choose a compressible site
Do not place a large introducer when the clinical need is met by a smaller multi-lumen catheter
anatomy: IJ and femoral are the usual sites; subclavian/axillary carry higher pneumothorax and noncompressible-bleeding risk with a large sheath.
The vein must comfortably accommodate an 8.5 Fr (or larger) sheath — confirm caliber and compressibility on ultrasound.
Distinguish compressible vein from pulsatile, noncompressible artery before puncture; the consequence of error scales with sheath size.
For IJ, note proximity of the carotid and the pleural dome at the base of the neck.
equipment: Introducer/Cordis kit with sheath, integrated dilator, guidewire, needle, and scalpel. This card matches the 8.5-9 Fr, 10 cm percutaneous sheath introducers with a hemostasis valve and side arm. If the kit in your hands is a different design, read its insert - assembly and removal sequences vary.
Sterile gown, gloves, mask, cap, and large sterile drape
Alcoholic chlorhexidine over 0.5% (alternative agent if contraindicated)
Ultrasound machine with sterile probe cover and sterile gel
Local anesthetic, syringe, and small needle
Sterile saline flush for the side port
Suture or securement device and sterile dressing
Sharps container and sterile towels
Confirmation workflow (chest x-ray) for IJ/subclavian/axillary placement
positioning: IJ: Trendelenburg if tolerated, head slightly turned away, neck not over-rotated.
Femoral: supine, leg slightly abducted and externally rotated if tolerated.
Set the ultrasound screen in your direct line of sight before sterile prep.
Optimize lighting and table height before opening the kit.
steps: Confirm indication for large-bore access and select the site by urgency, anatomy, and bleeding risk.
Ultrasound survey before opening the kit: confirm vein caliber, patency, and trajectory.
Prep and drape with full sterile barrier technique.
Anesthetize skin and deeper tissue along the planned tract.
Cannulate the vein under ultrasound guidance, maintaining needle-tip awareness.

Confirm the wire is venous before dilating: ultrasound in two planes - short axis showing the wire inside the vein and not the artery, long axis showing it tracking centrally. If the wire is not clearly seen, transduce or manometer before dilating. Blood colour and non-pulsatile flow do not confirm venous placement.

If any doubt remains, pass a small dilator or an 18 G catheter over the wire and transduce that before committing the 8.5 Fr dilator. In a peri-arrest patient there is no waveform to read, so ultrasound is the answer that still works.
Nick the skin through the dermis into subcutaneous tissue, blade flat against the wire and cutting away from it. An 8.5 Fr sheath needs a real nick or the tip accordions on the way in.
Advance the assembled dilator-and-sheath over the wire as a unit, using gentle rotation; do not force.
Remove the dilator and wire together while holding the sheath in place; confirm the wire is out intact.
Aspirate and flush the side port and cap or connect it immediately. The hub is never left open - an uncapped 8.5 Fr sheath is a large-bore conduit for air.
Secure the sheath and apply a sterile dressing.
Confirm position and assess for complications per site and local policy.
ultrasound: Confirm the vein is large enough for the sheath and compresses fully before puncture.
Use short-axis for vessel ID; long-axis helps track needle and wire if skilled.
Confirm the guidewire in the vein in two planes before dilating - the highest-stakes confirmation in the app given the dilator size. If the wire is not clearly seen, transduce before dilating.
For IJ, check lung sliding afterward as a rapid pneumothorax screen, but follow local confirmation standards.
confirmation: Side port aspirates and flushes easily
Guidewire and dilator removed intact
Sheath secured with sterile dressing
Appropriate imaging/confirmation obtained for the site
No evidence of arterial placement, pneumothorax, hematoma, or malposition
troubleshooting: Wire will not pass: stop, do not force; recheck needle position and angle, aspirate, use ultrasound, or repuncture.
Sheath tip peels back or kinks on advancement: the skin/tract nick is too small — withdraw, enlarge the nick, and re-advance over a controlled wire.

Arterial puncture with the needle only (18 G or smaller, not dilated): withdraw and hold firm pressure 5-10 minutes, longer if anticoagulated. After a neck puncture watch the airway for several hours - a carotid haematoma can obstruct late.

Dilator or catheter in an artery, or any device in the subclavian or axillary: leave it in place. Do not remove it and do not compress. Cap or transduce it so it neither bleeds nor entrains air, secure it against dislodgement, and call vascular surgery and interventional radiology now. Keep the patient flat and still. Removal with external pressure at a non-compressible site risks stroke, haemothorax, and uncontrolled bleeding.
Unsure whether you are in the artery or the vein: transduce it. Waveform and pressure answer in seconds; colour, non-pulsatile flow, and a blood gas do not.
Brisk bleeding around the sheath: apply pressure, assess coagulopathy, and confirm intraluminal placement.

Sudden hypoxia, hypotension, or cardiovascular collapse around an open hub: suspect air embolism - occlude the hub, left lateral decubitus head-down, 100% oxygen, and aspirate from a central lumen if one is in place.
Unstable after placement: consider pneumothorax, bleeding, arrhythmia, air embolism, or progression of underlying shock.
complications: Arterial cannulation with a large-bore sheath (surgical emergency)
Pneumothorax or hemothorax, especially with IJ/subclavian/axillary approaches
Hematoma or significant bleeding given the large tract
Air embolism through an uncapped large-bore sheath
Arrhythmia from wire or catheter irritation
aftercare: Keep the side port capped or connected at all times to prevent air embolism.
Label the sheath and date the dressing per local policy.
Review confirmation imaging before high-risk use if required by site/policy.

Removal is a procedure: patient supine or head-down, Valsalva or an expiratory hold as the sheath comes out, immediate occlusive dressing, and the patient stays flat afterwards. Most large-bore air embolism happens at removal, not insertion.
Remove the introducer as soon as large-bore access is no longer required.
Reassess the site for bleeding or hematoma after placement.
documentation: Introducer sheath (Cordis) placed for documented large-bore access indication.
Consent obtained when feasible; emergent need documented if not possible.
Site and side confirmed; full sterile barrier precautions used.
Ultrasound guidance used to identify the vein and guide cannulation.
Guidewire passed without resistance and removed intact with the dilator.
Side port aspirated and flushed; sheath secured with sterile dressing.
Placement confirmation and immediate complication assessment documented.
seniorPearls: The skin nick is the step most people underdo; an 8.5 Fr sheath needs a real nick or the tip accordions on the way in.
Dilation is irreversible — if you are not certain the wire is venous, you are not ready to dilate.
An uncapped large-bore sheath is an open conduit for air; cap or connect it the moment the dilator and wire come out.
references: American Society of Anesthesiologists. Practice Guidelines for Central Venous Access 2020. Anesthesiology. 2020;132(1):8-43. https://journals.lww.com/anesthesiology/fulltext/2020/01000/practice_guidelines_for_central_venous_access.9.aspx
Association of Anaesthetists. Safe Vascular Access 2025. Anaesthesia. 2025. https://associationofanaesthetists-publications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/anae.16727

Teleflex. Arrow percutaneous sheath introducer product and instructions-for-use reference. https://www.teleflex.com/usa/en/product-areas/vascular-access/central-access/percutaneous-sheath-introducer/index.html

CDC. Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections: summary of recommendations. 2011 guideline, page updated 2024. https://www.cdc.gov/infection-control/hcp/intravascular-catheter-related-infections/summary-recommendations.html
