shiftMode: This is a last-resort, time-critical trauma procedure. The criteria are below as numbers - if you are reasoning about whether the window has closed, it has.

Signs of life means any one of: a palpable pulse, a measurable blood pressure, spontaneous respiratory effort, pupillary reaction, spontaneous or purposeful movement, or organised cardiac electrical activity. None of the six, at any point since injury, and this is a resuscitation you are stopping rather than one you are opening.
CPR-duration windows (WTA 2024): under 15 minutes for penetrating trauma, under 10 minutes for blunt. Blunt arrest without signs of life is not an indication at any duration.
It presumes an operating theatre, a surgeon, and blood. Without a surgical destination this is not a bridge to anywhere.
Goals, in order: release tamponade, control intrathoracic haemorrhage, allow internal cardiac massage, and cross-clamp the descending aorta if subdiaphragmatic bleeding is the problem.
Left anterolateral thoracotomy at the 4th/5th intercostal space; extend across the sternum (clamshell) for right-sided or wider access.
Open the pericardium longitudinally and anterior to the phrenic nerve to relieve tamponade.
Massive transfusion, surgical backup, and a named destination activated before the incision, not after it.
indications: Penetrating thoracic trauma with signs of life at some point after injury and CPR under 15 minutes - the strongest indication and the one the outcome data rests on
Penetrating extrathoracic trauma within the same window: consider, but the yield is lower and the source may be abdominal
Blunt trauma arrest with signs of life and CPR under 10 minutes
Traumatic arrest with pericardial tamponade identified on ultrasound and a correctable source
Exsanguinating intrathoracic haemorrhage where an aortic cross-clamp is a bridge to the operating theatre
Exsanguinating abdominopelvic haemorrhage is a different branch: laparotomy, or Zone 1 REBOA where it is available and part of the local pathway - not thoracotomy
contraindications: Blunt trauma arrest with no signs of life. Survival is effectively zero and this is not indicated at any CPR duration.
No signs of life at any point since injury, for any mechanism
CPR beyond 15 minutes for penetrating or 10 minutes for blunt trauma
No operating theatre, surgeon, or blood available. Opening a chest nobody can repair is not a bridge.
Injuries clearly incompatible with survival, including devastating head injury
Adult criteria only. Paediatric resuscitative thoracotomy has its own algorithm and its own outcome data; use the paediatric trauma pathway.
anatomy: Left anterolateral approach at the 4th-5th intercostal space follows the rib's superior margin to avoid the neurovascular bundle.
The pericardium is opened longitudinally and anterior to the phrenic nerve, which runs along its lateral surface.

The descending thoracic aorta lies posteriorly against the spine. The oesophagus lies immediately anterior to it and is the structure most often clamped by mistake - an orogastric tube makes it identifiable by feel.
Clamshell extension across the sternum exposes both pleural cavities and the heart for wider access.
Crossing the sternum divides both internal mammary arteries. They will not bleed while there is no circulation and will bleed hard the moment there is one - find and ligate them.
equipment: Thoracotomy/clamshell tray: scalpel, Mayo scissors, rib spreader (Finochietto retractor)

An instrument that will actually divide the sternum: heavy trauma shears, a Lebsche knife, or a Gigli saw. Confirm which one is in your tray before the shift, because 'extend across the sternum' means nothing without it.
Vascular clamps (aortic and DeBakey-type) for cross-clamping and vessel control
Toothed forceps and large hemostats
Internal defibrillator paddles, and confirmation that they connect to your department's defibrillator - paddle and connector generations are not interchangeable
Suction and large volumes of gauze/laparotomy pads
Massive transfusion products and rapid infuser
Orogastric tube, to identify the oesophagus before clamping the aorta
Foley catheter or sutures for temporary cardiac wound control, and a skin stapler for rapid closure
Sterile gloves, gowns, eye protection, and face shields for the whole team - this is the highest blood-exposure procedure in the department
positioning: Patient supine with the left arm raised or abducted to expose the lateral chest.
Operate from the patient's left side for a left anterolateral thoracotomy.
Ensure continued airway management and ongoing resuscitation by the team.
Prep quickly; this is a time-critical procedure where speed and exposure dominate.
steps: Confirm the criteria in shiftMode by the numbers, then activate trauma surgery, massive transfusion, and the theatre.
Make a left anterolateral incision at the 4th-5th intercostal space along the superior rib margin, from the sternal edge to the table. Short incisions are the commonest reason this procedure fails.
Divide intercostal muscles and enter the pleura; place and open the rib spreader with its handle toward the axilla so it does not sit in the field.
Extend across the sternum (clamshell) if there is right-sided injury or you need wider exposure, then find and ligate both internal mammary arteries.
Open the pericardium longitudinally and anterior to the phrenic nerve, and evacuate clot to relieve tamponade. A tamponaded pericardium is tense and hard to pinch up - grasp and incise it.
Control cardiac wounds with finger pressure first, then a Foley balloon, staples, or sutures. Do not tie a suture around a coronary artery.

Internal cardiac massage two-handed. Internal defibrillation only if the rhythm is shockable, and at the low energy internal paddles use - commonly of the order of 10-20 J, and confirmed against your paddle and defibrillator instructions rather than assumed.

Cross-clamp the descending aorta only if the bleeding is subdiaphragmatic or you need to redirect what circulation there is to heart and brain. Retract the left lung anteriorly, open the posterior pleura, identify the aorta against the spine with the oesophagus anterior to it, and clamp under direct vision.
Say the clamp time out loud when you apply it and every five minutes after. Everything below the clamp is ischaemic, and its release is a second resuscitation.
Control intrathoracic bleeding and continue resuscitation with blood products.
Endpoint: no organised cardiac activity after tamponade release, haemorrhage control, and an aortic clamp is the answer the procedure gives you. Stop there.
Transport immediately to the operating room for definitive repair if circulation is restored.
ultrasound: Ultrasound before or around the arrest can identify tamponade and support the decision to proceed.

Cardiac standstill is not a free-standing reason to stop. Its place in the algorithm is narrow: in a patient in PEA with no signs of life, absent wall motion on a technically adequate view supports termination. In a patient with signs of life it changes nothing.
Never delay a clearly indicated thoracotomy to get a scan, and never repeat a scan to postpone the decision.
confirmation: Pericardium opened and tamponade relieved if present
Cardiac or great-vessel bleeding controlled
Aorta clamped under direct vision with the oesophagus identified, clamp time recorded, and central perfusion improved
Return of organized cardiac activity or perfusing rhythm as the resuscitation endpoint
Patient moving to definitive operative care without delay
troubleshooting: Cannot get exposure: the incision is too short or too high. Extend it to the table and across the sternum. Almost every failed thoracotomy is an inadequate incision.
Cannot find a cardiac wound after opening the pericardium: inspect the posterior surface and great vessels; lift the heart carefully.
Ongoing massive hemorrhage from the chest: pack, control the source, and cross-clamp the aorta while transfusing.
Sudden brisk bleeding after return of circulation in a clamshell: the internal mammary arteries. Look at the sternal edges first.
Clamp is on and nothing changed after a few minutes: question the clamp before the patient. It is probably on the oesophagus - check by feel against the orogastric tube - or the bleeding is above it.
Phrenic nerve in the way of pericardiotomy: open anterior to it to avoid injury.
Right-sided injury inaccessible from the left: extend to a clamshell for bilateral exposure.
No response after pericardial release and aortic clamp: reassess for non-survivable injury and the resuscitation endpoint.
complications: Iatrogenic injury to the heart, lung, phrenic nerve, or great vessels
Oesophageal injury from clamping the wrong posterior structure
Internal mammary bleeding after clamshell, unmasked by return of circulation
Coronary or aortic injury during clamping
Distal ischaemia below the clamp, and the reperfusion physiology when it comes off
Inadequate exposure leading to missed injury
Team blood-borne exposure during a rapid open procedure
Very high mortality given the underlying physiology
aftercare: Move immediately to the operating room for definitive repair if circulation returns.

Release the aortic clamp as early as the patient tolerates, and announce it. Reperfusion drops the pressure and returns the products of ischaemia to the circulation - the team should be ready rather than surprised.
Carry the clamp on and off times to the surgical team explicitly; they drive the ischaemic-time decisions you will not be there for.
Continue massive transfusion and correct coagulopathy, acidosis, and hypothermia.
Debrief the team and address occupational exposures after the resuscitation.
documentation: Resuscitative thoracotomy performed for [penetrating/blunt] trauma arrest meeting local criteria.
Mechanism, CPR duration in minutes, and which signs of life were present and when, named individually.
Procedure performed: thoracotomy with or without clamshell, pericardiotomy, hemorrhage control, aortic cross-clamp as applicable.
Aortic clamp application and release times documented.
Intraoperative findings and interventions recorded.
Resuscitation endpoint and disposition (OR vs. termination) documented against the criteria used.
Team exposures and debrief noted.
seniorPearls: The decision to open is the procedure. Applying the criteria correctly matters more than blade speed.
Open the pericardium anterior to the phrenic nerve and longitudinally; tamponade release is often the single highest-yield action.
The commonest technical failure is a small incision. Cut from the sternum to the table.
If you clamped and nothing changed, question the clamp before you question the patient.
This is a bridge, not a destination: it buys minutes to reach the OR, and only certain patients can cross that bridge.
references: Western Trauma Association. Adult Emergency Resuscitative Thoracotomy Algorithm and Procedure Guide. 2024. https://westerntrauma.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/ERT-Algorithm-Procedures.pdf

Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma. Emergency Department Thoracotomy: Practice Management Guideline. 2015. https://www.east.org/education-resources/practice-management-guidelines/details/emergency-department-thoracotomy

Name the institutional trauma algorithm that governs signs of life, CPR windows, REBOA availability, and termination, and confirm the thoracotomy tray contains a sternal-division instrument and compatible internal paddles.

visualAssets.title: Pericardiotomy & phrenic nerve
visualAssets.subtitle: Anterolateral incision level, rib-margin entry, and longitudinal pericardial opening anterior to the phrenic nerve.
visualAssets.caption: Placeholder: replace assetName with a bundled image when final reviewed artwork is added.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Visual must make the phrenic-nerve-sparing pericardiotomy and incision level unambiguous.

shiftMode: IO is a bridge, not a destination. Transition to definitive IV access when stable.
Tibia is the easiest site and the default when unsure. The humerus flows faster and delivers drug to the central circulation sooner in arrest, but it is mis-sited more often and dislodges during CPR.
In a responsive patient the lidocaine comes first, then the flush. Flushing an un-anaesthetised marrow is the painful step, and doing it first wastes the lidocaine.
Lidocaine 2%, preservative-free and epinephrine-free: 0.5 mg/kg to a 40 mg ceiling. Use the calculator - a flat adult dose can be many times the correct dose for an infant.
Nearly all IV medications and fluids can be given IO. Pressure bag or push-pull syringe for rapid infusion.
Aim to remove within 24 hours. Document site, time in, and reason for IO.
indications: Failed or impossible peripheral IV access in emergent setting
Cardiac arrest when IV access has failed or is not feasible - current adult guidance attempts IV first
Critically ill or injured patient requiring immediate vascular access
Pediatric resuscitation when IV access not rapidly obtained
Severe dehydration with vascular collapse
contraindications: Fracture in the target bone
Attempted or established IO access in the target bone within the past 48 hours
Overlying infection or burn at insertion site
Prosthetic joint or hardware at target site
Conditions with fragile bone (relative: osteogenesis imperfecta, severe osteoporosis)
Excessive tissue over the site, or landmarks that cannot be identified
anatomy: Proximal tibia: flat anteromedial surface, 1–2 cm distal and medial to the tibial tuberosity.
Proximal humerus: greater tubercle, arm adducted and internally rotated with the hand on the abdomen. Insert at 45 degrees to the anterior plane aimed posteromedially - not 90 degrees.
Distal tibia: medial malleolus, 1–2 cm proximal to the most prominent point.
In pediatrics the proximal tibia is preferred; the flat medial tibial surface is more accessible.
equipment: EZ-IO driver with needle sets: 15 mm (3-39 kg), 25 mm (40 kg and above), 45 mm (excess tissue, and the proximal humerus in most adults)
Antiseptic prep (chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine)
Gloves, eye protection
Normal saline flush syringes sized to the patient: 5-10 mL adult, 2-5 mL infant or child
Lidocaine 2%, preservative-free and epinephrine-free, for responsive patients
Extension tubing and IV setup
Pressure bag for fluid infusion
Stabilizer/dressing to secure IO needle
Sharps container
positioning: Proximal tibia: leg slightly externally rotated, small towel roll behind the knee.
Proximal humerus: arm adducted, hand on abdomen to internally rotate.
Stabilize the limb. Do not place your hand behind the insertion point.
steps: Identify the insertion site and confirm no contraindications at that limb.
Clean the site with antiseptic.
Stabilize the limb without placing your hand behind the target bone.
Select the needle by tissue depth rather than age: 15 mm for 3-39 kg, 25 mm for 40 kg and above, 45 mm for excess tissue and for the proximal humerus in most adults.
Attach the needle to the driver and touch the tip to bone. At least the 5 mm mark must be visible above the skin before you drill; if it is not, change to a longer needle.
Trajectory is site-specific: 90 degrees to bone at the tibia and distal femur; 45 degrees to the anterior plane, aimed posteromedially, at the proximal humerus.
Drill until loss of resistance (a subtle give or pop).
Remove the trocar, attach a syringe, and aspirate (marrow aspirate confirms placement but is not always obtained).

In a responsive patient give preservative-free, epinephrine-free lidocaine 2% at the weight-based dose on the max-dose card, slowly over about 120 seconds. Do not flush first - the marrow distension caused by the flush is the pain the lidocaine exists to prevent.
Allow about 60 seconds of dwell, then flush: 5-10 mL normal saline in adults, 2-5 mL in infants and children.
Connect IV tubing with extension set. Use pressure bag for rapid infusion.
Secure the needle and apply stabilizer dressing.
Document time of insertion, site, confirmation method, and complications.
confirmation: Needle stands upright without support after insertion
Loss of resistance felt during drilling
Marrow aspirate on syringe (not always present; absence does not rule out placement)
Saline flush flows freely without subcutaneous swelling
Medications and fluids infuse without extravasation
troubleshooting: No flow after insertion: ensure trocar removed, recheck position, attempt gentle flush. If extravasation seen, remove and attempt different bone.
Needle loose or wobbly: likely through-and-through cortex penetration. Remove and use a different site.

Significant pain in a responsive patient: give the weight-based lidocaine dose over 120 seconds and allow the 60-second dwell before flushing. About half the initial dose can be repeated if pain recurs.
Swelling at site: extravasation indicates malposition. Remove needle, compress, reassess compartment.
Lidocaine given but no effect in a small child: check the extension set. At paediatric volumes the set's dead space can hold most of the dose - prime it, or follow with the age-appropriate flush.
complications: Osteomyelitis (rare, risk increases if left in >24 hours)
Fracture (rare, more common with manual devices in pediatrics)
Pain during infusion in conscious patients
aftercare: Transition to peripheral or central IV access as soon as feasible.

Aim to remove the IO within 24 hours. Labelling permits up to 48 hours in selected patients aged 12 and over when no alternative access exists - do not pull a patient's only access to meet a deadline.
Document insertion time, site, removal time, and any complications.
Monitor insertion site for signs of infection, swelling, or compartment syndrome.
documentation: IO access placed at [site] using [device] for [indication].
Verbal/implied consent in emergent setting.
Site prepped, needle inserted with loss of resistance confirmed.
Flushed with [volume] normal saline without extravasation.
IO lidocaine given prior to infusion (if conscious).
Patient tolerated procedure. IO to be removed within 24 hours and transitioned to definitive access.
seniorPearls: IO is not a last resort. If you cannot get a peripheral line in a crashing patient in 90 seconds, drill.
The proximal humerus flows faster than the tibia in adults. Know both sites.
Lidocaine before the flush, not after. It takes three minutes including the dwell and it is the difference between a tolerable IO and one the patient fights.
Through-and-through is a real risk in peds. Use the correct needle length and stop at loss of resistance.
The 5 mm mark is worth more than any weight chart: it measures the thing that actually matters, which is how much needle is left after the tissue.
references: Teleflex. Arrow EZ-IO intraosseous vascular access procedure template, document MCI-2019-0395. https://www.teleflex.com/global/clinical-resources/documents/MCI-2019-0395_Arrow_EZ-IO_Intraosseous_Procedure_Template_LR.pdf

Teleflex. Arrow EZ-IO procedure competency template, MC-000270 rev 2c. 2021. https://www.teleflex.com/usa/en/clinical-resources/ez-io/documents/EM_IOS_EZIO%20Procedure-Competency-Template_MC-000270_rev2c.pdf
Teleflex. Arrow EZ-IO indications and contraindications data sheet. https://go.teleflex.com/EZUI-Procedure-Tray-Data-Sheet.html

American Heart Association. 2025 Guidelines for CPR and ECC: Adult Advanced Life Support, vascular access. 2025. https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support

visualAssets.title: Proximal tibia insertion site
visualAssets.subtitle: Palpate the tibial tuberosity. Move 1–2 cm distal and medial to the flat anteromedial tibial surface. This is the insertion point. Needle at 90 degrees to the bone.
visualAssets.caption: Replace assetName with reviewed artwork when available.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Do not place your hand behind the limb during drilling.

visualAssets.title: Proximal humerus insertion site
visualAssets.subtitle: Arm adducted, hand on abdomen (internal rotation). Palpate the greater tubercle — the most prominent lateral bony point of the shoulder. Needle at 90 degrees to the bone surface.
visualAssets.caption: Replace assetName with reviewed artwork when available.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Humeral IO flows faster than tibial in adults. Secure well — humeral IOs dislodge more easily.

agents.note: Preservative-free and epinephrine-free only. Adults are given 40 mg initially regardless of weight; infants and children get 0.5 mg/kg to a 40 mg maximum, which is the figure computed here.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Toxicity adds up, but the maximums are not interchangeable and two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling and keep the fractions adding to less than one - half the lidocaine maximum plus half the bupivacaine maximum is a full dose, not half of one. Everything counts: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
caveats: This is the dose to give, not a range to stay under.
At paediatric volumes the extension set's dead space can hold most of the dose. Prime the set or follow with the age-appropriate flush.
monitoring: Infuse slowly over about 120 seconds, then allow a 60-second dwell before flushing.
Flush volume is age-specific: 5-10 mL adult, 2-5 mL infant or child.
Reassess the site and the whole limb for extravasation before every infusion.

shiftMode: Superolateral approach is the most common. Medial approach is an alternative.
Always send fluid for cell count, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis.
Use sterile technique. A septic joint introduced by the tap is the complication that defines the case.

Tap before antibiotics when the patient is well enough to wait the few minutes it takes. If they are septic or in shock, give the antibiotics and tap after - blood cultures first, and say in the notes that the sample is post-antibiotic.
Ultrasound guidance increases success, especially in obese patients or small effusions.
Document appearance of fluid: clear, turbid, bloody, purulent.
indications: Acute monoarticular arthritis to evaluate for septic joint
Crystal arthropathy workup (gout, pseudogout)
Hemarthrosis evaluation
Symptomatic relief of tense effusion
Traumatic effusion with concern for intra-articular fracture or lipohemarthrosis
contraindications: Overlying cellulitis or skin infection at planned insertion site
Significant coagulopathy (relative; weigh risk vs. benefit if septic joint is suspected)
Prosthetic joint (consult orthopedics before tapping)
Patient refusal
anatomy: Superolateral approach: needle enters 1 cm superior and 1 cm lateral to the superolateral pole of the patella, directed toward the intercondylar notch.
Medial approach: needle enters at the midpoint of the patella on the medial side, directed posterolaterally.
The suprapatellar bursa communicates with the knee joint and is an alternative US-guided target.
Avoid the popliteal fossa (posterior neurovascular structures).
equipment: Sterile gloves and drape
Antiseptic prep (chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine)
Local anesthetic: 5 mL of 1% lidocaine, with a 25G needle for the skin wheal
18G needle and 20-60 mL syringe for aspiration

Sterile containers for the primary samples, with the remaining fluid inoculated into blood culture bottles. Tube colours and whether your laboratory accepts a culture bottle as the primary specimen are local - confirm with the lab that will run it rather than with a card.
Sterile dressing
Ultrasound with high-frequency linear probe (if available)
Hemostat (optional, for syringe exchange)
positioning: Patient supine with knee in slight flexion (15–20 degrees). A rolled towel behind the knee helps.
Relaxed quadriceps. The patella should be mobile.
Identify landmarks or use ultrasound to confirm effusion location.
steps: Confirm indication and obtain consent.
Position the knee in slight flexion. Identify landmarks or use ultrasound.
Prep the insertion site with antiseptic using sterile technique.
Anesthetize the skin and subcutaneous tissue with lidocaine down to the capsule.
Insert the 18G needle at the chosen approach, advancing toward the joint space while applying gentle negative pressure on the syringe.
Aspirate fluid. If using a large syringe, a hemostat can stabilize the needle during syringe exchange.
Remove as much fluid as clinically appropriate for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.
Remove the needle and apply sterile dressing.
Send fluid for cell count with differential, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis.
Document volume, appearance, and studies sent.
ultrasound: High-frequency linear probe placed over the suprapatellar recess (longitudinal) to confirm effusion.
Anechoic fluid collection confirms effusion. Complex or echogenic fluid may suggest infection or hemorrhage.
Use in-plane needle guidance for real-time visualization.
Particularly useful in obese patients or when clinical exam is equivocal.
confirmation: Synovial fluid aspirated into syringe
Knee effusion clinically reduced after aspiration
Fluid sent for appropriate laboratory studies
troubleshooting: Dry tap: reposition needle, use ultrasound guidance, consider smaller effusion or loculated collection.
Bloody aspirate: may be hemarthrosis or traumatic tap. Send for analysis. Lipohemarthrosis on gross inspection suggests intra-articular fracture.
Difficulty advancing needle: may be hitting bone. Redirect slightly.
Patient unable to relax quadriceps: coach relaxation, ensure adequate local anesthesia.
complications: Iatrogenic septic arthritis (rare with proper sterile technique)
aftercare: Instruct patient on signs of infection: increasing pain, redness, warmth, fever.
Keep dressing clean and dry for 24 hours.
Follow up on culture and crystal results.

If septic arthritis is suspected, treat and admit rather than waiting for a number. Sepsis or septic shock means empiric antibiotics immediately, before or without the aspirate - the tap comes first only when the patient can safely wait for it.
documentation: Knee arthrocentesis performed on [side] knee for [indication].
Informed consent obtained.
Site prepped with sterile technique. Local anesthesia administered.
Aspirated [volume] mL of [appearance] fluid using [approach].
Fluid sent for cell count, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis.
Patient tolerated procedure without immediate complication.
Sterile dressing applied.
seniorPearls: If you are debating whether to tap a hot swollen joint, tap it. Missing a septic joint is worse than a dry tap.
Ultrasound turns a frustrating blind procedure into a reliable one, in proportion to how much you have used it and how big the effusion is.
Clear straw-colored fluid at the bedside does not rule out infection. Send the labs.

There is no synovial white cell count that rules septic arthritis in or out. Above 50,000 raises the probability and does not confirm it; below 50,000 does not exclude it, particularly early, in the immunocompromised, and in prosthetic joints. Crystals do not exclude infection either - a patient can have gout and a septic joint in the same knee. Treat the patient, the culture, and the trajectory rather than the threshold.
references: European Bone and Joint Infection Society. Guideline for the management of septic arthritis in native joints (SANJO). J Bone Jt Infect. 2023;8(1):29-37. https://doi.org/10.5194/jbji-8-29-2023
Food and Drug Administration. Xylocaine and Xylocaine with epinephrine prescribing information. 2024. https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2024/006488Orig1s100lbl.pdf
Confirm specimen containers and order with the laboratory that will process them, and verify institutional policy on anticoagulation and prosthetic joint aspiration.

visualAssets.title: Superolateral approach
visualAssets.subtitle: 1 cm superior and 1 cm lateral to the superolateral pole of the patella. Direct the needle toward the intercondylar notch, posterior and slightly inferior.
visualAssets.caption: Replace assetName with reviewed artwork when available.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Avoid posterior approach (popliteal neurovascular bundle).

visualAssets.title: Suprapatellar recess ultrasound
visualAssets.subtitle: High-frequency linear probe placed longitudinally over the suprapatellar recess. Anechoic fluid between the quadriceps tendon and femur confirms effusion.
visualAssets.caption: Replace assetName with reviewed artwork when available.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Complex or echogenic fluid may indicate infection or hemarthrosis.

agents.note: Epinephrine buys a higher ceiling and a drier field. Avoid it in an end-arterial field unless local policy says otherwise.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than lidocaine or ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Toxicity adds up, but the maximums are not interchangeable and two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling and keep the fractions adding to less than one - half the lidocaine maximum plus half the bupivacaine maximum is a full dose, not half of one. Everything counts: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

Where it goes changes how fast it arrives. The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, designated by the clinical owner. The drug labels do not publish one universal figure per agent: they require individualisation by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary and is not the same as being safe.

shiftMode: Most anterior epistaxis is from Kiesselbach plexus (Little area) on the septum.
Start with direct pressure: pinch the soft part of the nose for 15 minutes continuously.
If a single bleeding point is visible, silver nitrate cautery may stop the bleed without packing.
If packing is needed, Rapid Rhino or Merocel sponge are first-line devices.
Always check vitals and hemodynamic stability. Posterior bleeds and anticoagulated patients can hemorrhage.
Patients discharged with packing need ENT follow-up for removal in 48–72 hours.
indications: Anterior epistaxis uncontrolled by direct pressure
Visible anterior bleeding source amenable to packing
Recurrent epistaxis requiring temporizing control
Post-cautery reinforcement when bleeding recurs
contraindications: Suspected posterior epistaxis (pack both if unavoidable, but involve ENT early)
Suspected nasal fracture with CSF leak (relative; manage with specialist)
Severe midface trauma requiring operative management
anatomy: Kiesselbach plexus (Little area): anterior septum, the most common source of anterior epistaxis.
Supplied by branches of anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, superior labial, and greater palatine arteries.
The nasal cavity narrows posteriorly. Packing must fill the anterior space to tamponade the vessel.
Direct packing along the nasal floor, not upward toward the cribriform plate.
equipment: Personal protective equipment (gown, gloves, face shield)
Headlamp or bright light source
Nasal speculum
Suction with Frazier tip
Topical vasoconstrictor (oxymetazoline spray or phenylephrine-soaked pledgets)

Topical anaesthetic: 4% lidocaine on cotton pledgets. That is 40 mg per millilitre, and nasal mucosa absorbs close to intravenous rates - 2-3 mL of it is 80-120 mg arriving fast. It counts against the same ceiling as anything injected, so do not keep re-soaking pledgets to hold the field.
Silver nitrate sticks (for cautery if appropriate)
Nasal packing device: Rapid Rhino, Merocel sponge, or ribbon gauze with petroleum jelly
Resorbable packing for patients with a bleeding disorder or on antithrombotic therapy - the guideline preference for that group, because removing a non-resorbable pack restarts the bleed

Sterile water to activate a Rapid Rhino's hydrocolloid coating, and a separate syringe of air for its cuff. The water is for the outside of the pack and the air is for the inside; saline goes in neither.
Antibiotic ointment (for gauze packing)
Kidney basin and gauze for blood management
Tranexamic acid (TXA) for topical use per local policy (e.g. 500 mg/5 mL injectable solution applied on a pledget or used to soak the pack)
positioning: Patient seated upright leaning slightly forward to prevent blood swallowing.
Have the patient blow out clots gently before examination.
Apply topical vasoconstrictor and anesthetic pledgets for 10–15 minutes before instrumentation.
steps: Ensure hemodynamic stability. Obtain IV access if significant bleeding or anticoagulation.
Apply personal protective equipment.
Have the patient blow out clots. Suction the nasal cavity.
Apply topical vasoconstrictor and anesthetic pledgets. Wait 10-15 minutes.
Remove pledgets and inspect with nasal speculum and headlamp to identify bleeding source.
If a single anterior point is identified and bleeding is controlled: apply silver nitrate to the site for 5-10 seconds. Do not cauterize both sides of the septum simultaneously (perforation risk).
If cautery fails or bleeding is diffuse: proceed to nasal packing.

Rapid Rhino: soak the pack in sterile water for at least 30 seconds to activate the hydrocolloid coating, insert along the nasal floor, then inflate the cuff slowly with air only, using the pilot cuff to judge it. Saline or water in the cuff is contrary to the manufacturer's instructions.
Merocel sponge: insert dry sponge along the nasal floor, then hydrate with saline to expand.
Ribbon gauze: layer gauze accordion-style from floor to ceiling of nasal cavity using bayonet forceps, coat with antibiotic ointment or petroleum jelly.
Confirm hemostasis. Check for posterior drainage in the oropharynx.
If bilateral packing is placed, monitor for hypoxia in high-risk patients.
confirmation: Active bleeding has stopped
No posterior drainage seen in the oropharynx on inspection
Packing is seated properly and not extruding
Patient hemodynamically stable
troubleshooting: Continued bleeding after packing: ensure packing fills the anterior cavity adequately. May need additional packing or posterior epistaxis management.
Posterior bleed suspected: blood draining in posterior pharynx despite adequate anterior packing. Place posterior balloon or consult ENT urgently.

Patient on an anticoagulant or antiplatelet: use the local measures first - pressure, vasoconstrictor, cautery, resorbable packing. Reversal or withholding the drug is not the opening move and is reserved for bleeding that is life-threatening. The decision to stop or reverse an antithrombotic belongs to the team that prescribed it or to haematology, jointly with ENT, and it is a decision with its own risks.
Vasovagal during packing: recline patient, maintain airway, resume when stable.
complications: Nasal septal necrosis or pressure injury (if packing too tight or left too long)
Sinusitis or toxic shock syndrome (rare, from prolonged packing)
aftercare: Discharge with packing in place. Arrange ENT follow-up for removal in 48-72 hours.

Antibiotics after packing are not an automatic prescription. The nosebleed guideline identifies both the benefit and the ideal duration as unresolved research questions, so follow a local policy if one exists and record the reasoning if you prescribe outside it. Toxic shock syndrome after nasal packing is rare, and routine prophylaxis has not been shown to prevent it.
Instruct patient to keep head elevated, avoid straining, nose blowing, and blood thinners if safe to hold.
Return precautions: recurrent heavy bleeding, difficulty breathing, fever, significant swelling.
documentation: Anterior epistaxis managed with [method: cautery / packing device].
Bleeding source identified on [side] anterior septum.
Bleeding-risk factors recorded: anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy with the agent and last dose, known bleeding disorder, liver disease, hypertension.
Topical vasoconstrictor and anaesthetic applied, with the agent, concentration, and approximate amount.
[Cautery performed / packing placed]: device, side, whether resorbable, and inflation medium if applicable.
Removal plan documented with the date and who will remove it.
No posterior drainage observed.
Patient hemodynamically stable. Discharged with ENT follow-up arranged and the transition of care recorded.
Return precautions given.
seniorPearls: Fifteen minutes of real continuous pressure stops most anterior bleeds. Patients never actually do this before they arrive.
If you cannot see the bleeding source, you cannot fix it. Suction, vasoconstrict, and light the field before touching anything.
Do not cauterize both sides of the septum. One side today, the other side never.
A posterior bleed masquerading as anterior packing failure will waste your time until you check the oropharynx.
references: Tunkel DE, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline: Nosebleed (Epistaxis). Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(1_suppl):S1-S38. https://doi.org/10.1177/0194599819890327
Smith+Nephew. RAPID RHINO usage instructions. https://rapidrhino.com/usage-instructions/
AAO-HNSF. Nosebleed guideline research needs. 2020. https://www.entnet.org/resource/cpg-nosebleed-epistaxis-research-needs/

Zahed R, et al. A new and rapid method for epistaxis treatment using injectable form of tranexamic acid topically: a randomized controlled trial. Am J Emerg Med. 2013;31(9):1389-1392. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajem.2013.06.043
Verify institutional policy on antibiotic prophylaxis with nasal packing, and read the instructions for use of the specific pack your department stocks.

agents.note: Applied topically on pledgets here, not injected. Nasal mucosa absorbs close to intravenous rates, so it counts against this same ceiling in full.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Toxicity adds up, but the maximums are not interchangeable and two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling and keep the fractions adding to less than one - half the lidocaine maximum plus half the bupivacaine maximum is a full dose, not half of one. Everything counts: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before soaking the first pledget - say it out loud.
Count every pledget against the running total; re-soaking a pledget is a second dose, not a top-up.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

Where it goes changes how fast it arrives. The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, designated by the clinical owner. The drug labels do not publish one universal figure per agent: they require individualisation by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary and is not the same as being safe.

shiftMode: Synchronized cardioversion delivers a shock timed to the R wave. Always confirm SYNC mode is on before shocking.
Unstable = cardiovert now. Stable = consider rate control, rhythm control, or elective cardioversion.
Signs of instability: hypotension, altered mental status, ischemic chest pain, acute heart failure.
Sedate the patient before cardioversion unless peri-arrest. Doses, monitoring, and rescue are on the procedural sedation card.
If the patient deteriorates into pulseless VT or VF, switch to defibrillation (SYNC off, max energy).
Initial biphasic energy: atrial fibrillation 200 J, atrial flutter 200 J, narrow-complex SVT 100 J, monomorphic VT with a pulse 100 J.

Those 200 J figures replace the old habit of starting low and climbing. A failed low-energy shock costs the patient another sedation and another shock. AHA states at least 200 J is reasonable for fibrillation and that 200 J may be reasonable for flutter, so the recommendation is stronger for fibrillation than for flutter.

Your defibrillator's manufacturer recommendation takes precedence over any figure above. Biphasic waveforms are not interchangeable and current AHA guidance defers to the manufacturer's stated dose - find out what your machine says before the night you need it.
Escalate toward the device maximum if a shock fails rather than repeating the same energy.
indications: Unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse (SVT, atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, monomorphic VT with a pulse)
Elective cardioversion of persistent atrial fibrillation or flutter, once the anticoagulation or imaging pathway below is satisfied
Wide complex tachycardia with hemodynamic compromise
contraindications: Pulseless VT or VF (requires unsynchronized defibrillation, not cardioversion)
Polymorphic VT (unsynchronized shock at defibrillation energy; the device cannot synchronize to it)
Known left atrial or left atrial appendage thrombus - an absolute contraindication to elective cardioversion

Elective cardioversion of atrial fibrillation lasting 48 hours or longer, or of unknown duration, without either three weeks of uninterrupted therapeutic anticoagulation or transoesophageal echo excluding thrombus
Digitalis toxicity-related arrhythmia (relative; cardioversion may precipitate refractory VF)
Multifocal atrial tachycardia (will not respond; treat underlying cause)
Sinus tachycardia (not an indication for cardioversion; treat the cause)
anatomy: Anterolateral pad placement: right parasternal and left lateral chest wall (V5-V6 position at the mid-axillary line).
Anteroposterior placement: sternum and left infrascapular area. May be superior for atrial fibrillation.

Do not place a pad over an implanted device generator. Keep at least 8 cm away, prefer anteroposterior, and confirm the separation your device and defibrillator manufacturers state rather than treating 8 cm as universal.
Any pacemaker or ICD needs interrogation after cardioversion. A shock can alter programming or damage the device, and this is the step everybody forgets.
Remove transdermal medication patches from the pad path. A metal-backed patch can arc and burn.
equipment: Defibrillator/cardioverter with SYNC capability, and knowledge of its recommended energies and its SYNC-persistence behaviour
Adhesive defibrillation pads (preferred over paddles)
Continuous cardiac monitor with 12-lead ECG capability

Sedation per the procedural sedation card, which carries the agents, doses, monitoring, and rescue requirements. Cardioversion is brief and intensely painful, which is the combination that card addresses directly.
Airway equipment including bag-valve mask, oral airway, suction, and intubation supplies at bedside
Pulse oximetry and continuous waveform capnography
IV access (ideally two sites)
Resuscitation medications (epinephrine, amiodarone, atropine) at bedside
Crash cart
positioning: Patient supine. Pads placed with good skin contact (shave excess chest hair if needed, wipe moisture).
Pads pressed down over their whole surface, and not overlapping ECG electrodes or medication patches - both cause burns and both raise impedance.
Clear the area around the patient before shock delivery.
Ensure monitor leads are connected and rhythm is visible.
steps: Confirm the indication: identify the rhythm, confirm hemodynamic instability or elective plan.
Obtain 12-lead ECG if time permits.
Establish IV access. Place monitoring (pulse ox, capnography, cardiac monitor).
Prepare airway equipment at bedside.
Apply defibrillation pads in anterolateral or anteroposterior position.
Administer procedural sedation per that card if the patient is conscious and not peri-arrest. Confirm depth before you charge, not after.
Select the energy for the rhythm, cross-checked against your defibrillator's recommended dose. Activate SYNC mode.
Verify SYNC markers are tracking R waves on the monitor.
Announce "Charging" and charge the defibrillator.
Perform a visual and verbal safety check: "I am clear, you are clear, everyone is clear."
Deliver the shock. Hold the shock button until the device fires (SYNC mode may have a brief delay).

Assess the rhythm immediately. If unsuccessful, escalate the energy rather than repeating the same one, and look at the screen to confirm SYNC before every shock - whether a device holds SYNC or drops it after a shock is configurable on current Philips and LIFEPAK platforms, so it is not something to remember about defibrillators in general.
If the patient becomes pulseless, immediately switch to defibrillation protocol.
confirmation: Post-shock rhythm is converted to sinus or target rhythm
Hemodynamic improvement (blood pressure, mentation, perfusion)
Repeat 12-lead ECG shows new rhythm
troubleshooting: Shock does not fire: SYNC mode waits for an R wave. If the rhythm is too irregular or amplitude is too low, the device may not fire. Try a different lead, increase ECG gain, or switch to unsynchronized defibrillation if the patient is deteriorating.
Rhythm unchanged after shock: escalate the energy, ensure good pad contact, try anteroposterior pad position.
Patient moves or remembers the shock: that is a sedation failure, not a cardioversion failure. Do not shock a conscious patient again without deepening sedation unless they are peri-arrest.
Patient deteriorates to VF or pulseless VT: immediately switch to unsynchronized defibrillation at max energy.
Post-cardioversion bradycardia: observe, atropine if symptomatic, transcutaneous pacing at bedside.
Recurrence of arrhythmia: consider antiarrhythmic medication before repeating cardioversion.
complications: Skin burns at pad sites, worse with poor contact, chest hair, or a shock delivered over an ECG electrode or medication patch
Thromboembolism (stroke) if atrial fibrillation cardioverted without adequate anticoagulation
Implanted pacemaker or ICD damage or reprogramming
aftercare: Monitor until the rhythm is stable and the sedation has resolved against the discharge criteria on the procedural sedation card. There is no evidence-based universal telemetry duration for cardioversion itself - the observation period is a local policy decision driven by the arrhythmia, the sedation, and comorbidity rather than a fixed number of hours.
Repeat 12-lead ECG.
Assess for chest wall discomfort and skin burns at pad sites.
Interrogate any pacemaker or ICD.

Anticoagulation after cardioversion: at least four weeks of uninterrupted therapeutic anticoagulation for anyone cardioverted from atrial fibrillation or flutter, whatever the pre-procedure duration, and then long-term by stroke risk rather than by whether the rhythm held.
An unstable patient cardioverted without the pre-procedure pathway still needs the post-procedure anticoagulation. The thromboembolic risk did not disappear because the cardioversion was necessary.
documentation: Synchronized cardioversion performed for [rhythm] with [indication].
Pre-procedure rhythm documented on 12-lead ECG.
Atrial fibrillation or flutter: duration, and which pre-procedure pathway applied - anticoagulation, imaging, or urgent without either.
Sedation: [agent, dose, route]. Adequate sedation achieved.
SYNC mode confirmed. [Energy] J delivered via biphasic defibrillator, with the device model recorded.
Post-shock rhythm: [rhythm]. Hemodynamics [stable/improved].
Patient tolerated procedure without immediate complication.
Post-procedure 12-lead ECG obtained. Monitoring, device interrogation, and anticoagulation plan documented.
seniorPearls: Look at SYNC on the screen before every shock. Whether your device holds it or drops it depends on the model and its configuration, so the habit that survives every platform is checking rather than remembering.
The shock button delay in SYNC mode confuses people. Hold the button until it fires.
The first shock is the one most likely to work. Do not spend it on a low energy chosen out of caution.
Anteroposterior pad placement is better for atrial fibrillation. If anterolateral fails, switch before escalating energy.
Do not cardiovert sinus tachycardia. Find and fix the cause.
If the rhythm is polymorphic VT, treat it as VF: unsynchronized defibrillation, not synchronized cardioversion.
Interrogate the pacemaker afterwards. It is the step that gets left out, and the patient goes home with a device nobody checked.
references: American Heart Association. Electrical Cardioversion Algorithm, 2025 CPR and ECC Guidelines. 2025. https://www.heart.org/-/media/CPR-Files/CPR-Guidelines-Files/2025-Algorithms/Algorithm-ACLS-Electrical-Cardioversion-250514.pdf

American Heart Association. Part 9: Adult Advanced Life Support, 2025 CPR and ECC Guidelines - synchronized cardioversion energy and manufacturer dose deference. 2025. https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support
Joglar JA, et al. 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation. Circulation. 2024;149(1):e1-e156. https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001193

Read your defibrillator's operating instructions for its recommended cardioversion energies, SYNC-persistence configuration, and implanted-device clearance. Philips HeartStart Intrepid and Stryker LIFEPAK 15 are examples: https://www.stryker.com/content/dam/stryker/ems/resources/operating-instructions/international/3314911-030_int-eng_lifepak_15_operating_instructions.pdf
Verify institutional cardioversion and sedation protocols.

shiftMode: Needle aspiration, incision and drainage, and abscess tonsillectomy are all effective. Aspiration is the usual bedside choice because it is the one a non-surgeon can do safely; it is not established as superior. Follow the local ENT preference where there is one.
Decide first whether this patient can have anything done at the bedside at all. See contraindications - the airway question comes before the technique question.
The danger: the internal carotid artery lies posterolateral to the tonsil, typically 2-2.5 cm from the mucosal surface.
Limit needle depth to 1 cm with a guard (cut syringe sheath or tape) to prevent deep penetration.
Aspirate at the point of maximal fluctuance or bulging, usually the superior pole of the tonsil.
Always have suction ready. These patients aspirate pus.
If you cannot aspirate pus but clinical suspicion is high, consider CT with contrast or ENT consultation.
indications: Clinically suspected peritonsillar abscess (unilateral tonsillar swelling, uvular deviation, trismus, muffled voice)
Confirmed peritonsillar abscess on imaging or clinical exam
Failed outpatient antibiotic therapy for peritonsillar cellulitis progressing to abscess
contraindications: Any airway warning sign: stridor, drooling or inability to handle secretions, respiratory distress, a tripoding or sniffing posture, or hypoxia. These patients need a controlled airway plan and ENT or anaesthesia involvement, not a needle at the bedside.
Severe sepsis or septic shock - resuscitate and involve ENT and critical care; drainage still needs to happen, but not as an unmonitored bedside procedure.
Concern for deep space neck infection extending beyond the peritonsillar space: neck swelling, torticollis, trismus out of proportion, or pain on neck movement. Image and consult ENT or surgery.
Pulsatile mass or bruit suggesting vascular anomaly (get imaging first)
Severe trismus preventing adequate visualization - you cannot aim a needle at what you cannot see. Sedation or operative drainage.
Patient unable to cooperate (relative; consider procedural sedation, and if sedation is needed then the monitoring on the procedural sedation card applies)

Bedside drainage belongs in a space with suction, oxygen, monitoring, and airway equipment immediately to hand. If the room does not have them, that is a contraindication to the room, not to the procedure.
anatomy: The peritonsillar space lies between the tonsillar capsule and the superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle.
The internal carotid artery runs posterolateral, typically 2–2.5 cm from the pharyngeal mucosal surface.
Most PTAs collect at the superior pole of the tonsil, between the anterior tonsillar pillar and the soft palate.
Uvular deviation is typically away from the affected side.
The palatine tonsil, anterior and posterior pillars, and soft palate are key landmarks.
equipment: Headlamp or good overhead light
Tongue depressor

Topical anaesthetic spray. If you use a benzocaine product such as Cetacaine, keep to the shortest labelled spray - about one second - and never repeat it freely: benzocaine sprays carry an FDA warning for methaemoglobinaemia, which can be fatal, and the mouth and pharynx absorb quickly. A lidocaine-based topical avoids the issue entirely and is the safer default.
Local anesthetic: lidocaine 1% with epinephrine, 3 mL syringe, 25G needle
Aspiration: 18G needle on a 10 mL syringe
Needle guard: tape or cut syringe cap placed 1 cm from needle tip
Suction with Yankauer tip, tested before you start
Oxygen, monitoring, and airway equipment in the room
Kidney basin
Specimen cup for culture
Methylene blue available in the department if benzocaine is used - it is the treatment for methaemoglobinaemia, and cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen is the sign
positioning: Patient seated upright, leaning slightly forward.
Good light source directed at the oropharynx.
Tongue depressor in the non-dominant hand.
Suction immediately available.
Have the patient open mouth maximally. If trismus limits opening, topical anesthetic and gentle approach or sedation may be needed.
steps: Confirm the diagnosis clinically: unilateral tonsillar swelling, uvular deviation, muffled voice, trismus.
Apply topical anesthetic spray to the area of planned aspiration.
Inject local anesthetic (1% lidocaine with epinephrine) into the mucosa overlying the abscess. Aspirate first to exclude vascular puncture.
Attach an 18G needle to a 10 mL syringe. Place a needle guard at 1 cm from the tip.
Insert the needle at the point of maximal fluctuance (usually the superior pole, at the junction of the anterior pillar and soft palate).
Aspirate while advancing slowly up to 1 cm only.
If pus is obtained: aspirate as much as possible. Send sample for culture.
If no pus is obtained: redirect the needle slightly inferior or medial. A second attempt at the middle pole may be tried.
If no pus after 2–3 attempts: consider CT to confirm abscess vs. cellulitis, or consult ENT.
After drainage, have the patient gargle and spit. Reassess the oropharynx.
ultrasound: Intraoral ultrasound (endocavitary probe with a cover) can identify the abscess collection and confirm depth.
Transcutaneous submandibular approach may help identify large collections.
Particularly useful when clinical exam is equivocal or prior aspiration was dry.
confirmation: Purulent material aspirated
Improvement in uvular deviation and tonsillar swelling
Patient reports subjective improvement in swallowing and pain
Reduced trismus
troubleshooting: Dry tap: reposition needle to a different quadrant. Consider imaging if repeated attempts fail.
Trismus limiting access: topical anesthetic, consider procedural sedation, or refer to ENT for operative drainage.

Significant bleeding: apply pressure with gauze, maintain suction, most minor mucosal bleeding is self-limited. Pulsatile or brisk bleeding is a different problem - secure the airway and get ENT and vascular help.
Cyanosis or low saturations after a benzocaine spray, not improving with oxygen: methaemoglobinaemia. Stop the agent, give oxygen, send a co-oximetry level, and treat with methylene blue.
Large abscess with rapid re-accumulation: ENT consultation for incision and drainage or tonsillectomy.
complications: Aspiration of pus into the airway
Injury to the internal carotid artery (prevented by needle depth guard)
Infection spread to deep neck spaces
aftercare: Oral antibiotics: amoxicillin-clavulanate or clindamycin. Follow institutional guidelines for dose and duration.
Pain management: NSAIDs and paracetamol.

A single dose of a corticosteroid - dexamethasone is the agent studied - is a reasonable adjunct for pain and trismus. The evidence is limited and heterogeneous, and it supports one dose rather than a multi-day tapering pack. The earlier instruction to consider a methylprednisolone dose pack is not supported and has been removed.
Confirm the patient can swallow before discharge. Watch them drink something. Inability to tolerate oral intake is the commonest reason a discharged patient comes back.
Encourage oral hydration. Soft diet.
ENT follow-up within 2-3 days for reassessment.
Return precautions: worsening pain, inability to swallow, difficulty breathing, fever, neck swelling.
documentation: Peritonsillar abscess drainage via needle aspiration performed.
Informed consent obtained.
Topical and local anesthesia applied to [side] peritonsillar area.
Needle inserted at superior pole with depth guard at 1 cm.
Aspirated [volume] mL of purulent material. Sent for culture.
Patient tolerated procedure without complication.
Antibiotics prescribed. ENT follow-up arranged. Return precautions discussed.
seniorPearls: The needle guard is not optional. The carotid is 2 cm away. You only need 1 cm of depth.
If the patient cannot open their mouth, do not force it. Sedate or consult ENT.
Most PTAs are at the superior pole. If your first aspiration is dry, try there before giving up.
These patients look terrible but get dramatically better within minutes of drainage. That immediate relief is diagnostic and therapeutic.
references: Windfuhr JP, et al. Clinical practice guideline: tonsillitis II. Surgical management. Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol. 2016;273(4):989-1009. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00405-016-3904-x

DailyMed. Cetacaine Topical Anesthetic prescribing information, including the methemoglobinemia warning. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=af1773c5-5d5b-4278-b551-30ad2df6d5b5
Chau JKM, et al. Corticosteroids in peritonsillar abscess treatment: a blinded placebo-controlled clinical trial. Laryngoscope. 2014;124(1):97-103. https://doi.org/10.1002/lary.24283
Verify institutional antibiotic guidelines, the topical anaesthetic on your formulary, and ENT referral pathways.

agents.note: Epinephrine buys a higher ceiling and a drier field. Avoid it in an end-arterial field unless local policy says otherwise.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than lidocaine or ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Toxicity adds up, but the maximums are not interchangeable and two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling and keep the fractions adding to less than one - half the lidocaine maximum plus half the bupivacaine maximum is a full dose, not half of one. Everything counts: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

shiftMode: X-ray finds most glass, metal, gravel, and bone. It is not a rule-out: small fragments, some glass, and some ceramic are missed, and a negative film with a persistent story means ultrasound or CT, not reassurance.
X-ray does not reliably show wood, plastic, or thorns at all. Ultrasound is the bedside tool for those.
Adequate anesthesia and a bloodless field make the difference between a controlled extraction and a dig.
A digital tourniquet has to come off. Use a device you cannot miss, write the time down, and check the finger after - see equipment and aftercare. Retained tourniquets have cost fingers.
If you cannot find it in a reasonable time or it is near critical structures, stop and refer.
Document what you found, what you removed, and what imaging showed. If retained FB is possible, tell the patient.
Tetanus status and wound infection risk should be addressed at every visit.
indications: Known or suspected retained foreign body in soft tissue
Wound with mechanism suggesting foreign body (glass, wood, metal)
Non-healing wound or recurrent infection suggesting retained material
Patient-reported foreign body sensation
contraindications: Foreign body near major neurovascular structures requiring operative exploration
Deep foreign body not accessible with bedside techniques
Foreign body that is asymptomatic, deeply embedded, and not causing infection (may be observed in select cases)
Inadequate anesthesia or equipment for safe removal
anatomy: Knowledge of local neurovascular anatomy is essential for safe exploration.
Hand and foot foreign bodies are near tendons, nerves, and vessels in tight compartments.
Plantar foot: flexor tendons, digital nerves, and plantar fascia are at risk during deep exploration.
The depth and tissue plane of the foreign body dictate the approach. Imaging helps plan.
equipment: Local anesthetic: 1% or 2% lidocaine, with epinephrine where the field allows it
Syringe and needle for anesthesia (25-27G)
Antiseptic prep
Sterile gloves and drape
Scalpel (#11 or #15 blade)
Hemostats (mosquito and Kelly)
Fine-tipped forceps (splinter forceps or Adson)
Iris scissors
Needle driver
Wound irrigation supplies (saline, 18G angiocath on 30-60 mL syringe)

Digit tourniquet, and it must be a device that cannot be forgotten: a brightly coloured commercial ring tourniquet, or a glove finger or Penrose secured with a large clamp left hanging outside the drape. A rolled glove finger tucked under a dressing is the arrangement that gets left on.
A clock or timer, and something to write the application time on - the drape, the notes, or the patient's chart
Ultrasound with high-frequency linear probe
Suture material for closure if needed
positioning: Position the affected area for optimal access, lighting, and comfort.
Digit procedures: apply the tourniquet only after the field is prepped, record the time of application out loud and in writing, and leave the device visible outside the drape.
Ensure the patient is comfortable and the field is well-lit.
steps: Obtain history: mechanism, timing, material type, symptoms since injury.
Examine the wound. Assess for signs of infection, neurovascular status distally.
Image the area: X-ray for radiopaque materials, ultrasound for radiolucent objects. A negative X-ray with a story that still fits does not close the question.
Mark the foreign body location on the skin using imaging guidance if needed.
Anesthetize the area with local or regional block as appropriate.
Prep and drape the wound.
Digits: apply the tourniquet now, record the time, and leave the device visible.
If the foreign body is visible or superficial: extract with forceps.
If deeper: make a small incision over the marked location. Blunt dissect along tissue planes using hemostats.
Use ultrasound in real-time to guide your approach to deeper or radiolucent foreign bodies.
Grasp and remove the foreign body. Inspect it for fragmentation.
Irrigate the wound with normal saline.
Reassess the wound. Obtain post-removal imaging if fragmentation is suspected.
Remove the tourniquet and say so out loud. Record the removal time and the total tourniquet time.
Confirm the digit is perfused: capillary refill and colour, compared with the neighbouring finger.
Close the wound if appropriate (clean, non-infected, within time window). Leave contaminated or infected wounds open.
Apply appropriate dressing - and confirm again that the tourniquet is not under it.
ultrasound: High-frequency linear probe (10–15 MHz) provides best resolution for superficial foreign bodies.
Foreign bodies appear as hyperechoic structures, often with posterior shadowing (glass, metal) or reverberation artifact.
Wood may appear as a hyperechoic linear structure with dirty shadowing.
Scan in two orthogonal planes to localize in 3D.
Real-time ultrasound guidance during extraction improves success for deep or small foreign bodies.
confirmation: Foreign body visualized and removed intact
Post-removal imaging shows no retained fragments (if indicated). Negative imaging is not proof of complete removal when the object may be radiolucent or fragmented.
Wound irrigated and inspected
Tourniquet removed, removal time recorded, and the digit confirmed pink with normal capillary refill
Neurovascular status intact after removal
troubleshooting: Cannot locate foreign body: reimage with ultrasound, try a different scanning plane, consider CT for deep or small objects. Ultrasound sensitivity falls with depth, small size, and operator inexperience, so a negative scan is not an answer on its own.
Fragmented foreign body: remove what is accessible, image to assess residual, discuss with patient and consider specialist referral.
Significant bleeding during exploration: apply direct pressure, tourniquet for digits, consider specialist referral for deep structures.
Foreign body near nerve or tendon: stop if safe extraction is not possible. Refer to hand surgery or appropriate specialist.
Tourniquet time approaching 20-30 minutes: stop, release, and reassess. There is no foreign body worth a digit.
complications: Digital ischaemia or amputation from a tourniquet left in place - the reason the removal step is written as its own step with its own time record
Excessive tissue damage from prolonged exploration
aftercare: Confirm the tourniquet is off before the patient leaves the room. If a handover happens mid-procedure, the tourniquet is the first thing handed over.

Tetanus: assess the wound as clean-minor or dirty-major and the immunisation history separately, and give vaccine, tetanus immune globulin, or both accordingly. See the laceration repair card, which carries the full decision.
Antibiotics for contaminated wounds, bite wounds, or immunocompromised patients per guidelines.
Wound care instructions: keep clean, dressing changes, elevation.
Return precautions: increasing pain, redness, swelling, drainage, fever, or a cold or discoloured digit.
If retained FB is possible: disclose to patient, arrange follow-up, document discussion.
documentation: Foreign body removal performed from [location].
Informed consent obtained.
Pre-procedure imaging: [modality] showing [finding], and the limits of that modality for this material noted.
Local anesthesia administered: agent, concentration, and volume. Sterile technique used.
Tourniquet [used/not used]; if used, device type, application time, removal time, and total tourniquet time recorded, with post-removal perfusion documented.
Foreign body identified and removed: [description of object].
Wound irrigated with [volume] normal saline.
Post-procedure neurovascular status intact.
[Wound closed with X / wound left open for healing by secondary intention].
Tetanus status addressed with the vaccine and immune globulin decision recorded. Return precautions and follow-up discussed.
seniorPearls: If you are digging for more than 15 minutes, you are not removing a foreign body. You are creating a bigger wound.
Ultrasound finds much of what X-ray misses, and misses things too. Neither is a rule-out; the history is.
The tourniquet on a finger transforms a bloody mess into a clean field. It also transforms a finger into a stump if it stays on. Write the time down.
Telling a patient there might be a retained fragment is better than them finding out later.
references: National Patient Safety Agency. Reducing risks of tourniquets left on after finger and toe surgery. 2010. https://www.cas.mhra.gov.uk/ViewandAcknowledgment/ViewAttachment.aspx?Attachment_id=101035
American College of Emergency Physicians. Sonoguide: Foreign Body Localization. 2020. https://www.acep.org/sonoguide/procedures/foreign-bodies/
American College of Radiology. Appropriateness Criteria: Suspected Osteomyelitis, Septic Arthritis, or Soft Tissue Infection - 2022 Update. https://acsearch.acr.org/docs/3094201/Narrative/
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Clinical Guidance for Wound Management to Prevent Tetanus. 2025. https://www.cdc.gov/tetanus/hcp/clinical-guidance/index.html
Verify institutional wound management and antibiotic prophylaxis guidelines.

shiftMode: Target: C5-C7 nerve roots between anterior and middle scalene muscles.

Hemidiaphragmatic paresis is volume-dependent, not universal: 20 mL produced it in 100% of patients in the randomised trial that figure comes from, and 5 mL in 45%. At the 10-15 mL on this card, expect it often and not always - and avoid the block in severe COPD or respiratory failure regardless.
Use low volume (10-15 mL) and always visualize needle tip to avoid intravascular/intraneural injection.
Work out the maximum in milligrams and in millilitres before you draw up, and say it out loud. The calculator is on this card.
Aspirate before each increment and give the dose in stages. Aspiration and incremental injection are the two things that catch a needle that has found a vessel.
Decide what you will do if the block does not work before you start - not afterwards, when the patient is still in pain and the allowance is spent.
indications: Shoulder dislocation (pre-reduction)
Proximal humerus fracture
Clavicle fracture (lateral third)
Complex shoulder or upper arm lacerations
contraindications: Contralateral phrenic nerve palsy or severe baseline pulmonary disease (e.g., severe COPD)
Infection over the injection site
Patient refusal or inability to cooperate
Local anesthetic allergy
Patient refusal, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
A pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory. Document it before you block; a deficit nobody looked for beforehand becomes the block's deficit afterwards.

Antithrombotic therapy is not an automatic prohibition for a superficial, compressible block. anatomy: The brachial plexus roots (C5-C7) exit between the anterior and middle scalene muscles.

The carotid artery and internal jugular vein are medial to the anterior scalene.

steps: Perform a pre-block neurovascular exam of the upper extremity.
Apply continuous cardiac monitoring and pulse oximetry, and confirm lipid emulsion availability, before injecting any volume.
Prep the lateral neck with chlorhexidine.
Place the linear probe transversely over the supraclavicular fossa to identify the subclavian artery and brachial plexus ('bunch of grapes').
Trace the brachial plexus cephalad until it forms the 'stoplight' sign between the anterior and middle scalenes.
Insert the needle in-plane from posterior to anterior (lateral to medial).
Advance the needle through the middle scalene muscle until the tip rests in the interscalene groove.
Aspirate to ensure no vascular puncture, then inject 1-2 mL to confirm spread (hydrodissection).
Inject the remaining anesthetic in 3-5 mL aliquots, aspirating between each, targeting the space around C5-C7.
Withdraw the needle and apply a sterile dressing.
ultrasound: Identify the carotid artery medially and the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) superficially.
The anterior scalene muscle lies deep to the SCM and lateral to the internal jugular vein.
The middle scalene muscle is lateral to the anterior scalene.
The nerve roots appear as hypoechoic, round structures in the fascial plane between the two scalene muscles.
confirmation: Anechoic fluid seen spreading around the C5-C7 nerve roots in the interscalene groove.
Patient reports subjective loss of sensation over the shoulder/deltoid.
Motor weakness in shoulder abduction (deltoid) and elbow flexion (biceps).
Spread on the screen is not success. It tells you where the drug went, not whether the patient is blocked.
Test the target's own territory before the procedure starts: light touch or cold in the distribution, and motor function where the nerve has one, compared against the other side.
Give the agent its onset time before judging. Lidocaine is 5-10 minutes; bupivacaine and ropivacaine are 15-30. A block called failed at 5 minutes was never tested.

shiftMode: Target: Superficial cervical plexus as it emerges behind the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle.
Provides anesthesia to the anterior/lateral neck, clavicle, and skin over the shoulder.
Work out the maximum in milligrams and in millilitres before you draw up, and say it out loud. The calculator is on this card.
Aspirate before each increment and give the dose in stages. Aspiration and incremental injection are the two things that catch a needle that has found a vessel.
Decide what you will do if the block does not work before you start - not afterwards, when the patient is still in pain and the allowance is spent.
indications: Clavicle fractures
Laceration repairs of the anterior/lateral neck or earlobe
Internal jugular vein cannulation (pain control)
contraindications: Infection at the injection site
Allergy to local anesthetic
Patient refusal, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Infection over the injection site
A pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory. Document it before you block; a deficit nobody looked for beforehand becomes the block's deficit afterwards.

Antithrombotic therapy is not an automatic prohibition for a superficial, compressible block. Current guidance asks three questions instead: can the site be compressed, how vascular is it, and what would a haematoma there do. Answer those, and follow local policy - do not transpose a neuraxial interval onto a block that does not need one.
anatomy: The plexus wraps around the posterior border of the SCM at approximately its midpoint.
The external jugular vein typically crosses the SCM near this level.
equipment: High-frequency linear ultrasound transducer
25G or 27G needle (1.5 inch)
Local anesthetic (5-10 mL, e.g., 1% lidocaine or 0.25% bupivacaine)
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation, applied and then left to dry - the drying time is the part that gets skipped and the part that does the work.
Sterile gloves, and for any ultrasound-guided block a single-use sterile probe cover with sterile gel.
IV access, blood pressure, ECG, and pulse oximetry in place before the needle goes in. This is a major block; the label asks for IV access for exactly this class.
Oxygen, suction, an airway kit, and resuscitation equipment in the room rather than down the corridor.
20% lipid emulsion located, not assumed. If you cannot say where it is, you are not ready to inject.
positioning: Patient supine, head turned away from the side being blocked.
steps: Place the transducer transversely over the mid-SCM.
Identify the posterior border of the SCM.
Insert the needle in-plane from posterior to anterior.
Aspirate, then inject 5-10 mL of anesthetic in the fascial plane immediately deep to the posterior border of the SCM.
ultrasound: SCM is the large superficial muscle. Deep to it is the levator scapulae or scalenes.
The plexus often appears as a small hyperechoic cluster at the posterior edge of the SCM.
confirmation: Anesthetic spreading along the posterior border of the SCM, separating the fascial layers.
Numbness over the neck and clavicle.
Spread on the screen is not success. It tells you where the drug went, not whether the patient is blocked.
Test the target's own territory before the procedure starts: light touch or cold in the distribution, and motor function where the nerve has one, compared against the other side.
Give the agent its onset time before judging. Lidocaine is 5-10 minutes; bupivacaine and ropivacaine are 15-30. A block called failed at 5 minutes was never tested.
troubleshooting: If the needle tip is not visible, use hydrodissection with small amounts of saline.
Avoid going too deep to prevent a deep cervical plexus block or phrenic nerve block.
Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Work out what allowance is left on the calculator on this card before drawing up anything more.

Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. The options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia. More of the same is how the ceiling gets crossed.
Pain on injection, paraesthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Those three are the warning that the tip is where it should not be, and none of them is a reason to push harder.
complications: Phrenic nerve block (if injection is too deep/voluminous)
Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
Bleeding or haematoma at the injection site
Nerve injury, usually transient and occasionally not

aftercare: Monitor for 30 minutes, especially for dyspnea (phrenic nerve involvement).
Protect the insensate part. Pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts - they cannot feel the injury that a blocked limb collects.
Motor block means the limb cannot be trusted for weight-bearing, and that is a fall risk in an older patient. Say so at handover as well as to the patient.
Tell the patient when it will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does, not after.

A block does not hide compartment syndrome, but it changes how it announces itself: a rising analgesic requirement, or pain breaking through a block that was working, is the sign. Write that in the notes and say it at handover so the next person is watching for the right thing.
Return precautions: numbness or weakness lasting longer than you told them to expect, new or escalating pain, or redness at the injection site.
documentation: Consent, indications, anesthetic volume/type, absence of complications.
Side and level, named unambiguously. Wrong-side blocks happen to careful people, and the note is where the side gets fixed in writing before the needle moves.

Needle type and gauge, the approach, and whether ultrasound guidance was used in-plane or out-of-plane.

The neurological examination before the block and again after it, with any pre-existing deficit recorded as pre-existing.

shiftMode: Target: Fascial plane between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles.
Provides analgesia to the anterior abdominal wall (parietal peritoneum and skin).
Work out the maximum in milligrams and in millilitres before you draw up, and say it out loud. The calculator is on this card.
Aspirate before each increment and give the dose in stages. Aspiration and incremental injection are the two things that catch a needle that has found a vessel.
Decide what you will do if the block does not work before you start - not afterwards, when the patient is still in pain and the allowance is spent.

Abdominal wall abscesses or lacerations
Post-operative abdominal pain
contraindications: Infection at the injection site
Allergy to local anesthetic

TAP is classified as a superficial nerve procedure for antithrombotic purposes, not a deep one, so the earlier 'deep fascial plane' rationale was wrong.
