Bilateral block without a recalculated combined maximum dose (both sides share one limit)
Patient refusal, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Infection over the injection site
A pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory. Document it before you block; a deficit nobody looked for beforehand becomes the block's deficit afterwards.

Antithrombotic therapy is not an automatic prohibition for a superficial, compressible block. Current guidance asks three questions instead: can the site be compressed, how vascular is it, and what would a haematoma there do. Answer those, and follow local policy - do not transpose a neuraxial interval onto a block that does not need one.
anatomy: The lateral abdominal wall consists of three muscle layers: external oblique (superficial), internal oblique (middle), and transversus abdominis (deep).
The nerves supplying the abdominal wall run in the plane between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
equipment: High-frequency linear or curvilinear transducer
Regional block needle (21G or 22G, 80-100mm)

Local anaesthetic: 20-30 mL per side of 0.25% bupivacaine or 0.2% ropivacaine. Those are the strengths the labels supply, and at 30 mL a side they put a bilateral block well under the concentrations that caused trouble in the TAP pharmacokinetic studies. Do not dose up to the calculated ceiling here - read the caveat on the dose card.
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation, applied and then left to dry - the drying time is the part that gets skipped and the part that does the work.
Sterile gloves, and for any ultrasound-guided block a single-use sterile probe cover with sterile gel.
IV access, blood pressure, ECG, and pulse oximetry in place before the needle goes in. This is a major block; the label asks for IV access for exactly this class.
Oxygen, suction, an airway kit, and resuscitation equipment in the room rather than down the corridor.
20% lipid emulsion located, not assumed. If you cannot say where it is, you are not ready to inject.
positioning: Patient supine, abdomen exposed.
steps: Place the transducer transversely on the lateral abdominal wall, midway between the costal margin and the iliac crest (mid-axillary line).
Identify the three muscle layers.
Insert the needle in-plane from anterior to posterior (or vice-versa).
Advance the needle until the tip pops through the fascia of the internal oblique into the TAP plane.
Aspirate, then inject 20-30 mL of anesthetic in 3-5 mL increments with repeat aspiration, staying under the calculated maximum dose.
ultrasound: Look for the 'three stripes' of muscle. The deepest stripe (transversus abdominis) sits right above the peritoneum/bowel.
confirmation: Anechoic fluid spreading linearly, creating a black elliptical space separating the internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
Spread on the screen is not success. It tells you where the drug went, not whether the patient is blocked.
Test the target's own territory before the procedure starts: light touch or cold in the distribution, and motor function where the nerve has one, compared against the other side.
Give the agent its onset time before judging. Lidocaine is 5-10 minutes; bupivacaine and ropivacaine are 15-30. A block called failed at 5 minutes was never tested.

Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Work out what allowance is left on the calculator on this card before drawing up anything more.

Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. The options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia. More of the same is how the ceiling gets crossed.
Pain on injection, paraesthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Those three are the warning that the tip is where it should not be, and none of them is a reason to push harder.
complications: Intraperitoneal injection / Bowel puncture (if needle goes too deep)
Liver/spleen injury (rare, if performed too high)
Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
Bleeding or haematoma at the injection site
Nerve injury, usually transient and occasionally not
Block failure, which is common enough to plan for rather than to be surprised by
aftercare: Monitor for LAST for 30-60 minutes.
Protect the insensate part. Pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts - they cannot feel the injury that a blocked limb collects.
Motor block means the limb cannot be trusted for weight-bearing, and that is a fall risk in an older patient. Say so at handover as well as to the patient.
Tell the patient when it will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does, not after.

A block does not hide compartment syndrome, but it changes how it announces itself: a rising analgesic requirement, or pain breaking through a block that was working, is the sign. Write that in the notes and say it at handover so the next person is watching for the right thing.
Return precautions: numbness or weakness lasting longer than you told them to expect, new or escalating pain, or redness at the injection site.
documentation: Consent, confirmation of the three muscle layers, visualization of spread in the correct plane, absence of intraperitoneal injection.
Side and level, named unambiguously. Wrong-side blocks happen to careful people, and the note is where the side gets fixed in writing before the needle moves.

Needle type and gauge, the approach, and whether ultrasound guidance was used in-plane or out-of-plane.

The neurological examination before the block and again after it, with any pre-existing deficit recorded as pre-existing.
The bleeding-risk assessment and what it concluded, including any antithrombotic the patient is taking.

steps: **Intraoral Approach (Preferred):**
Palpate the infraorbital foramen extraorally with your non-dominant index finger.
Apply topical anesthetic to the buccal mucosa above the maxillary canine/first premolar.
Retract the upper lip.
Insert the needle into the mucobuccal fold above the canine/first premolar, directing it superiorly toward your palpating finger.
Stop before hitting the bone or entering the foramen.
Aspirate, then inject 2-3 mL of anesthetic.
Keep the palpating finger over the foramen for the whole injection. It is the physical stop that prevents the needle travelling past it, and taking it away is what allows an orbital trajectory.

Intraoral approach: advance parallel to the long axis of the second premolar toward the fingertip, roughly 1.5-2 cm in an adult, and stop there. A shallower angle points at the orbit rather than at the foramen, and depth without a direction is the part that goes wrong.
Never advance toward or into the orbit, and never past the palpating finger. Stop for pain, paraesthesia, or any resistance you did not expect.
ultrasound: Can be used extraorally to identify the foramen (a break in the hyperechoic maxillary bone) and guide an extraoral injection.

steps: Apply topical anesthetic to the mucosa posterior to the last molar.
Palpate the greatest concavity on the anterior border of the mandibular ramus (coronoid notch) with your non-dominant thumb.
Visualize the pterygomandibular raphe (a vertical fold of tissue medial to the ramus).
Approach with the syringe barrel resting over the premolars of the *opposite* side of the mouth.
Insert the needle at the midpoint between your thumb and the raphe, about 1 cm above the occlusal plane of the lower molars.
Advance until you contact bone (usually ~20-25 mm).
Withdraw 1-2 mm, aspirate carefully (high vascularity area), and inject 1.5-2 mL.
As you withdraw the needle halfway, inject the remaining 0.5 mL to block the lingual nerve.

confirmation: Profound numbness of the lower teeth, lower lip, and ipsilateral anterior 2/3 of the tongue (lingual nerve).

shiftMode: Target: A 'ring block' around the base of the ear to hit the greater auricular, lesser occipital, and auriculotemporal nerves.
Provides complete anesthesia of the auricle (except the external auditory canal and concha).
Work out the maximum in milligrams and in millilitres before you draw up, and say it out loud. The calculator is on this card.
Aspirate before each increment and give the dose in stages. Aspiration and incremental injection are the two things that catch a needle that has found a vessel.
Decide what you will do if the block does not work before you start - not afterwards, when the patient is still in pain and the allowance is spent.
indications: Complex ear lacerations
Auricular hematoma drainage
contraindications: Infection at the injection sites
Allergy to local anesthetic
Patient refusal, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Infection over the injection site
A pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory. Document it before you block; a deficit nobody looked for beforehand becomes the block's deficit afterwards.

Antithrombotic therapy is not an automatic prohibition for a superficial, compressible block. Current guidance asks three questions instead: can the site be compressed, how vascular is it, and what would a haematoma there do. Answer those, and follow local policy - do not transpose a neuraxial interval onto a block that does not need one.
anatomy: The ear is supplied by multiple nerves coming from different directions.
A diamond-shaped ring of subcutaneous anesthetic around the base of the ear blocks them all.
equipment: 25G or 27G needle (1.5 inch)
Local anesthetic (5-10 mL of 1% lidocaine or bupivacaine, WITHOUT epinephrine to avoid cartilage ischemia)
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation, applied and then left to dry - the drying time is the part that gets skipped and the part that does the work.
Sterile gloves, and for any ultrasound-guided block a single-use sterile probe cover with sterile gel.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you inject. A small block still uses a drug with a systemic ceiling.
positioning: Patient seated or in lateral decubitus with the affected ear up.
steps: Cleanse the skin around the entire ear.
1. Insert the needle just inferior to the earlobe. Inject subcutaneously while tracking anteriorly in front of the tragus.
2. From the same inferior puncture site, track the needle posteriorly behind the earlobe, injecting subcutaneously along the mastoid.
3. Insert the needle just superior to the ear. Track anteriorly to meet the first track.
4. From the superior puncture site, track posteriorly to meet the second track.
You have now created a complete diamond or ring of anesthetic around the base of the ear.
ultrasound: Not used.
confirmation: Complete numbness of the auricle (pinna).
Spread on the screen is not success. It tells you where the drug went, not whether the patient is blocked.
Test the target's own territory before the procedure starts: light touch or cold in the distribution, and motor function where the nerve has one, compared against the other side.
Give the agent its onset time before judging. Lidocaine is 5-10 minutes; bupivacaine and ropivacaine are 15-30. A block called failed at 5 minutes was never tested.
troubleshooting: If the concha (the bowl of the ear) remains painful, it is because it receives innervation from the vagus/facial nerves deeper inside. A local wheal directly in the concha may be needed.
Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Work out what allowance is left on the calculator on this card before drawing up anything more.

Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. The options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia. More of the same is how the ceiling gets crossed.
Pain on injection, paraesthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Those three are the warning that the tip is where it should not be, and none of them is a reason to push harder.
complications: Cartilage necrosis (if epinephrine is used, though controversial, best avoided)
Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
Bleeding or haematoma at the injection site
Nerve injury, usually transient and occasionally not
Block failure, which is common enough to plan for rather than to be surprised by
aftercare: Routine wound care or compression dressing (for hematomas).
Protect the insensate part. Pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts - they cannot feel the injury that a blocked limb collects.
